utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I greet you all. It's case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are today Tuesday, the 4th of July. I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom; the representatives from the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, Mr. Coric who is back again today, and I should also like to welcome all the people working in the courtroom. We have an hour and a half now and we will pursue the examination-in-chief until our next break, and without more ado, I shall turn the floor over to Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Manolic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is your voice okay?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to start this morning by taking you to the book -- your book, which I believe you have with you. If it will assist you we can put it on the screen. I understand you have a copy of your book with you. It's Exhibit P 09673.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for purposes of the English translation, you should have a bundle of materials that was given to you. I'm going to start with the excerpt that is titled at the top of the page "Key to breaking up: policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina." I do not believe it's in the large bundles, I'm told by my case manager, but they were handed out to the Chamber a few minutes ago. And it is the first bundle -- first piece of it we'll be talking about is, again, on the top of the page, it says: "3. Key to breaking up: policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina," and it corresponds to pages 317 to 321 of the Croatian-language book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please put it on the monitor so I don't have to search through the book now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Either way, whatever is best for you, sir. If you could put up, please, page 317, then, of Exhibit P 09673. Although I'm not sure, Mr. Manolic, whether it won't be easier for you ultimately to use your book, but it's up to you. We're starting at page 317 of the B/C/S material. Sir, on that page under that heading that I've just referred to several times, it says this: "In his 22 April, 1994, interview to Globus, Manolic explained once again - but this time in more detail than ever - what were the main differences between him and President Tudjman with regard to policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina." Further on, the next two paragraphs -- at the end of the next paragraph, it says: "My supporters -" that is yours, Mr. Manolic - "My supporters, as it is known, were opting for an alliance with Muslims and for integral Bosnia and Herzegovina within the borders defined after World War II. Tudjman and Milosevic, however, agreed on division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Everything that followed after negotiations took place -- which took place in Karadjordjevo in March of 1991 showed clearly that Tudjman and Milosevic agreed on partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." Now, with that in mind, sir, and looking back at the first paragraph that I directed your attention to, where it says the main differences between you and President Tudjman with regard to the policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, can you tell us, sir, again, what were the main differences between you and President Tudjman on this policy?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I adhered to the results of the referendum which was held, in favour of an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was a legal referendum, and the entire people voted, both the Croat people and the Muslim people. Starting from this, I constantly advocated the standpoint that there are no realistic possibilities of dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially not when tensions escalated at the point in time when the republic Herceg-Bosna was established. It's impossible for there to be two states on a single territory, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an integral state and, within that state, a new republic. This was illogical, it was impossible, it was not viable. It could have been viable for a brief period of time until a new solution was found. President Tudjman wanted to annex Western Herzegovina to Croatia. This was a wish. It was the request of those seven or eight municipalities, the names of which we read out yesterday. The people who lived in those areas felt that their future and their security could be found within the borders of the Republic of Croatia. However, wishes are one thing and realistic possibilities of realising your desire are something else, and there were no realistic preconditions for realising that wish. Therefore, this was in dispute between me and President Tudjman, and we never agreed on it until the very last day, until the Washington agreements were signed which put an end to this dilemma and created the federation of Croats and Muslims in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Continuing down the same page beyond where we've read already, it says: "Most certainly subjects of the Karadjordjevo talks were changes of internal borders and increase of Croat and Serbian state territories ..." Can you tell us what was -- what was your understanding, what was being discussed in terms of not internal borders but the increase of Croat state territory? How was that going to be done and where was that going to be done?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible to increase the territory of any state without entering onto the territory of another state. The same situation obtained here. It was impossible to increase the territory of Croatia or to thicken the crescent, the croissant, without impinging upon the neighbouring state. There are only two ways of achieving something like this; either through agreements or by force. There weren't very many conditions for the forcible solution, although there was violence, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, it says: "Tudjman wanted to incorporate West Herzegovina into Croatia. He counted also on some other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the most important issue was the annexation of Herzegovina." Why was the annexation of Herzegovina the most important part?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was ethnically the purest Croatian territory. It was inhabited by ethnic Croats, and it is territorially adjacent to the Republic of Croatia, so it was most natural to annex that part, but as we know, this never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you refer to talks in Graz between Mate Boban and Radovan Karadzic in 1992. At the end of that paragraph you say, that these "... interests can be adjusted only to the detriment of Bosniaks and central government in Sarajevo." Why could those interests only be adjusted to the detriment of Bosniaks and the Central Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the two sides, the Serbs with Karadzic at their head and the Croats with Mate Boban at the head, and they had a written agreement - the results show this - they agreed on spheres of interest in that area, and this impinged on the central issue of the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could continue down. Skip one paragraph, please, until you find this language -- in the English excerpt, Your Honours and for the courtroom, I'm turning to page 2 of the English translation of that excerpt, second paragraph: "According to this, the official state policy -- the official Croatian policy wanted to make the government in Sarajevo weaker, and this can be proved without problem. Even before the conflict between Muslims and Croats began, a decision on pulling out all Croat ministers from the central government was adopted by Zagreb." Can you please tell the Judges more about how these ministers were pulled out of the government.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was a mistake, made by President Tudjman first of all. He agreed on this thesis of withdrawal. We as the Croatian state had recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign state. It was our neighbouring state. So it was not logical that this government representing Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign state, that one should withdraw one's ministers, Croats, from that government. This means opening up space for the aggressor, the enemy, which was the greatest Serbian policy of Karadzic. The defenders of Bosnia-Herzegovina would find it very difficult to defend it. There was no reason not to adhere the results of the referendum about the integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the decision made by the Croatian government to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign state in the area. So this decision on withdrawing ministers ran counter to these two decisions, and as we have seen, it was not a good decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, further on --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- the result of that withdrawal was weakening the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this helped the Greater Serbian aggressor; that is Karadzic. That was a mistake that President Tudjman made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. We've had a technical problem with LiveNote on the Defence side since the beginning of the session, and we had hoped that it would be solved within a few minutes, and we wanted to continue, but, Your Honour, it's getting more and more difficult because there are certain passages that we need to follow in LiveNote and I wonder if we can get some information perhaps about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it only your screen that's a problem? This will be seen to in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just further, a bit down that same page, you refer to this happening a second time. You say, "The second time, the decision to withdraw Croat ministers was adopted." Do you recall approximately when that occurred and why that was done?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was when there was already a conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, an armed conflict in that area. Mr. Boban and Herceg-Bosna defended this by saying that the Croatian ministers could not be in the central government as long as there was a war between the Muslims and the Croats, and the Muslims were in fact holding the central power in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of course, this withdrawal was not realistic, and it was not in the interest of the Croatian people, because weakening the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that point in the face of the main aggressor was also weakening the overall Croatian position in relation to that aggressor. There was an aggression not only against Bosnia-Herzegovina but also against Croatia, and the aggressor was one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I could ask you to turn several pages in your book until you find the paragraph that starts: "It is obvious that the main idea ..." And for the English readers, I'm now -- we're going to page 4 of that same excerpt. So if you can find, sir -- or it can be put on the screen, either way. If you can find a page or two down from where we were, where it says, "It is obvious that the main idea ..." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you see it, sir? Page 320 of your book, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It says: "It is obvious that the main idea of the Croatian state policy was brought down to a partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina independently from any other circumstances. Annexation of Herzegovina to Croatia was really the guiding idea of the Croatian state policy in the last two years." Now, with that in mind, could I ask you to skip a paragraph and go down one paragraph, where it says, "Actually, main goal of Tudjman's policy was the realisation of the Banovina Croatia borders." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was that in fact the policy of Tudjman and Susak and Boban?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think that Susak and Boban did nothing without the knowledge of President Tudjman as regards their activities. Gojko Susak - and you have something I said about it in the text - said that the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was the party through which this policy was being implemented, was only a branch of the HDZ of the Republic of Croatia, and this is what was impermissible. This is the link that gave rise to considerable difficulties for us in defending our standpoint that we did not - we as Croatia - did not participate in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But these elements indicate that, contrary to this, the overall policy was being prosecuted by Croatia from Zagreb with respect to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna as a republic. Its existence and its establishment would not have happened had it not been in line with the ideas of President Tudjman, Gojko Susak, and the others who supported them. And in Zagreb, we can see Gojko Susak, the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, Vice Vukojevic, who was working on the same plan and who was more influential in the legislative sphere, and Mr. Pasalic, who joined the same line. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the main implementers of this policy were Boban, Kordic, and the third echelon, including the accused here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the bottom of that page, sir, in the next paragraph, you go on to say that you had initially shown some constraint in criticising President Tudjman directly, but then at the end of that paragraph you said that there was no reason any longer to do that. You make reference to the -- apparently a speech by President Tudjman at the Deputies Club, HDZ Deputies Club. Can you tell us what you can recall about the speech by Mr. Tudjman in which you say here, "The president took complete responsibility for policy towards BiH"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Until that point in time, we had pointed out that Gojko Susak and, as we called it, the Herzegovina lobby, were the main exponents of this policy of Herceg-Bosna, the conflict with the Muslims, the weakening of the central government, and the setting of demands for the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, in a speech of his President Tudjman made to the Deputies Club in the Croatian parliament - and this is where we definitely parted ways - he said that the policy being implemented in Bosnia and Herzegovina and towards Bosnia and Herzegovina was his policy. He took on himself this responsibility by saying it was his policy. Gojko Susak, as the minister of defence, was said by Tudjman to be a good minister because he was implementing Tudjman's policy. And this is evidence of who was responsible for what was happening in that area at that time. In my public speeches, I should say, throughout this period I tried to bypass President Tudjman as the one who was responsible for this policy which I felt was disastrous, catastrophic for the Croatian state as a whole. I tried to give him room for manoeuvre. He, as the president of Croatia, as the commander-in-chief of the Croatian army, could always represent things differently than what was actually happening. And you will find this in all the transcripts and in my book. And I wish to emphasise the positive elements in searching for a solution. More than once, especially after the Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement, I emphasised those elements which could have produced positive results in resolving the problem we were facing in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir, just in terms of -- for the record, when you make reference to Tudjman-Izetbegovic agreement, can you give us a bit more information about which agreement you're talking about and the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This agreement which I mentioned was reached later on in 1994 when a definite solution was sought before the Washington Agreement. So it was the end of 1993, sometime in September, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I next ask you, sir, to go to page 246 of your book. And for the courtroom and the English version excerpt, it is the one that says -- starts with "6. Policy regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina." On that page, if you start with page 246 of your book and if you go down about to the fourth paragraph, can you find a passage, please, sir -- also fourth paragraph on the English version: "Firstly, it was concluded that the question regarding the creation of Herceg-Bosna, as a state in a state, had no basis." It's on page 247, third paragraph of your book. And can you tell the Judges, please, a bit more about why the creation of Herceg-Bosna as a state in a skate had no basis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no theoretical possibility, nor was there any practical possibility. If we were going to create a separate state within a state, this would bring us into conflict with the legal and constitutional order of that state. That same constitutional order established the external borders but also the internal order. So of course such a policy would come into conflict with this. I always pointed out that this was an unrealistic policy which would do no good either to the Croatian state or to the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The biggest mistake that was made when Herceg-Bosna was established as a republic was that the Croatian population in Bosnia and Herzegovina was split up. The Croats living in Central Bosnia, in Bosnian Posavina, those Croats were, in a way, cut off from Herceg-Bosna as a state and an entity, so that this segment, by separating itself out, weakened the entire Croatian body in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Croatian Catholic clergy and many other opposition parties opposed such a policy, because it's well known that the area of Banja Luka and Bosanska Posavina had about 150.000 Catholics, parishioners in that area. And when Bishop Komarica protested against this division because of this policy, and we also have to say because of the Greater Serbian aggression, but also because of Boban's policy who was calling upon the Croats from that area to come to the Adriatic, to come Istria, to find a new home there, this was the biggest mistake that was made in relation to the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also I think it weakened the position of the Croatian state in relation to the aggressor and in view of the subsequent development of events in the area which is still being resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, sir, you mention, several lines down, "Some moves of certain people showed that a separate state was really being created in Herceg-Bosna." Can you give us any examples of the moves? You say "some moves," example of the moves that showed that? And when you say "certain people," if you can identify any people, the persons that you would include in that group.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is widely known that the people through whom such policy was pursued were Boban, whom I mentioned, Kordic, and people from that establishment. Those were the people who were the proponents of that policy at the time. I think that we also have to compare this to the period when Kljuic was president of the HDZ, and then Brkic, who served in that office for a brief period of time. They opposed such policy precisely because of the element that I motioned, because such policy split apart the interests of Croatian people in that territory. When I criticised Susak by telling him that he pursued an erroneous policy and that such policy took into account only the interests of Croats in Herzegovina, whereas my policy was a policy which took into account the entirety of interests of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is where we differed mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, if you could go to page 249 of your book, second paragraph on that page, and the third page of this particular excerpt in the English translation. It says: "Herzegovina does not at all suit at least one of these three sides, and that is the Muslims, who are in the majority in this country, 44 per cent. The annihilation is something the Serbian radicals want, thus achieving the plan of 'Greater Serbia,' but I can't claim that on the Croatian side there aren't those who see the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the solution either." And then if you go down, you'll see further you just made reference, which I was going to ask you, but you talk about Kljuic and Brkic. Do you see that in your book on that page? The next -- middle of the following paragraph, sir, do you see the names Kljuic and Brkic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in Croatian politics in Bosnia and Herzegovina there must be room for the thoughts of Kljuic and Brkic and Boban. I meant to say that we should take into account what Kljuic thought that was in the interest of the entire Croatian people, and this was also the position taken by Kljuic. This is why they were against very firmly defined borders between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you can see this in one portion of the Boban-Karadzic agreement reached in Graz. You see that there is something quite dishonest that the Serbs forced Boban to accept, because they stepped aside from the ethnic principle. There were no Serbs living in that area. However, they wanted to gain the territory in that corridor for themselves. And this was impermissible, because if you adhere to one principle in your policies, then you have to comply with that principle in your policy as a whole in all of the territories to which your policy applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the one paragraph down below -- skip a paragraph, I believe, after the references to Kljuic and Brkic, and you see this passage, please: "The most Zagreb can do is to advocate a change in the policy that has resulted in the fatal consequences for the Croatian nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Again, sir, could you please tell the Judges -- describe the policy -- describe the policy that resulted in the fatal -- in fatal consequences for the Croatian nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the armed conflict with the Muslims. What happened there was that there was an erroneous assessment of the Herzegovina lobby in the first place. I can say that, because President Tudjman had some dilemmas concerning that problem, namely that the Croatian forces would be able to defeat the enemy in armed conflict very soon and then pave the way for their policies. However, that didn't happen. What happened was that the opposing side, the Muslim side, which proposed the central government in Bosnia and Herzegovina, continually became stronger. It had a huge human potential that it used throughout the war, and its potential increased during the war. It was only handicapped by the fact that on one hand it was surrounded by Croatian policies, and on the other hand it was surrounded by Serbian policies, which didn't allow it to reach the full potential or to achieve the full potential in terms of armament that would supply all of the human resources that the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had at its disposal. So this is where they made a mistake. It was an erroneous assessment concerning the ratio of forces that existed in that territory, and that opened the way for the armed conflict with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, a moment ago you used the term "Herzegovina lobby," which I'm not sure that phrase or term has been used before in the trial. Can you tell the Judges, when you say "Herzegovina lobby," what is that and who comprised it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like all lobbies, in theoretical sense it means that all people supporting the same ideas join forces in order to defend the ideas and goals that they're going to try to achieve. This was the Herzegovina lobby, and in Croatian political scene that included those people that I mentioned. Those are the people who accepted that the conflict with the Muslims was a good solution and would further the policy that they created. Those people included Boban, Kordic, and others, other leaders at the time. Naturally, they had support in certain municipalities, in the grassroots. So not only at the top within the HVO and Croatian army. No, they also had their supporters in municipalities, that is to say in the field, but it also had some opponents, because otherwise it would have been impossible for the Croatian civil party to be established, and it was established in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, could I next ask you please to turn to page 262 of your book. And for those using the English translation, it is in the excerpt that starts on the top of the first page, "2. The Croatian-Muslim war in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Excerpt titled, "2. The Croatian-Muslim war in Bosnia-Herzegovina." On page 262 of your book, sir, if you see this. You make references at the end of the paragraph to "... the architects and organisers of this for the Croatian fate almost suicidal war." And when you say architects and organisers of this, do you have in mind the same people you've been telling us about this morning or do you want to add or say anything more about the architects and organisers of this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this refers to the same people who were the proponents of this policy and its architects, its authors. Their main mistake was that they made an erroneous judgement about the balance of forces, and as a result of that they entered into an armed conflict with the Muslims. And this is where all the tension arose. The defenders of this policy kept saying that it wasn't us who started this conflict, it was the Muslims, the opposite side. And it is very difficult now to establish who started it first. It is clear why this conflict arose. It is clear now what led to it, but who fired the first bullet, was it the Muslims against Croats, or was it vice versa? It's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you said just now it is clear why this conflict arose, that is regardless of, as you say, who fired the first bullet, it is clear why this conflict arose, can you give us more information about that? In what way is it clear?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear based on everything that led to it, all the preparations. It was clear based on the agreement reached between Boban and Karadzic, because if you enter into negotiations with an aggressor, somebody who was an aggressor until just recently prior to that, this means that this was a radical change that took place, that they made an erroneous judgement as to the balance of forces, and the conflict with Muslims broke out. The front against the aggression wasn't completely closed either. It was still smouldering. There were still UNPA zones existing in Croatia where the Serbs were dominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned in the immediate following passage or two, you mentioned the concentration camps for Muslims on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. During this time, sir, did you condemn the existence, operation of those concentration camps?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we refer to fatal mistakes that were done, that we, then -- I firstly am referring to the armed conflict. That was the starting point. And then the camps, prisons, and torture facilities were just what led after that first initial mistake, what resulted after that first initial mistake. There were several of us within the Croatian Assembly which consistently opposed that policy and the resulting mistakes. It wasn't a sin that we discussed it. What was the sin were the goals of the conversation led by President Tudjman and the others. This is what was criminal, and this is what produced the consequences that we discuss to this day; problems that were created in the past and that we continue to discuss to this day, including before this International Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to correct Mr. Scott, who in his question said: "You spoke of concentration camps at the time." And then what Mr. Manolic said in that interview does not refer to concentration camps at all. It was the journalist who mentioned concentration camps in his question. I would like to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's correct, Mr. Scott. I noticed that there is the phrase stating "the HVO camps." You said "concentration camps." It was you who said it, and this is where the problem arose, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't see -- I don't see the issue, Your Honour. In the book, at least the translation that I have, it says: "In this context, in an interview with Globus on the 10th of September, 1993, Manolic spoke for the first time, although not entirely openly, about the concentration camps for Muslims on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Then he goes on to talk about them, and the next line, couple of lines down, it says: "I am aware of the fact that the HVO camps make the Croats in Bosnia appear evermore like the Serbs." So I'm not sure what the problem is. It clearly identifies concentration camps. Those are Mr. Manolic's words. He clearly says they're HVO camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I think the point that Mr. Praljak is making is that the word "concentration" does not appear to be in the Croatian version, although it is in the English translation. At least, that's what I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that's issue, I'll be happy to ask the witness if he can clarify from his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard, I hope, this exchange in the last moment or two. When you look in the Croatian-language original in your book about that statement, does the word "concentration" -- do the words "concentration camps" occur in your language in that passage?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we need to say that the establishment of concentration camps was to an extent a secret. The public wasn't actually informed about the creation of such camps. You must be aware of this. I think that there was a commission of the Red Cross, or perhaps the Red Crescent, which established that there existed an HVO camp within Bosnia. I believe that it was in Dretelj. So I think that we really shouldn't debate whether it was a concentration camp or not. The fact is that people were kept there. Some of them were civilians, and some of them were prisoners. This is what the commission established. And this is what produced the reaction of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior and other institutions aimed at shutting down that concentration camp. I don't know whether I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, in your book you speak of the camps. At the time you were in Zagreb; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what was the information reaching the politicians in Zagreb, politicians such as you, about the existence of prisons in Bosnia-Herzegovina? What information did you have available at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already pointed out that to a certain extent this was secret, and this was not discussed publicly in Zagreb. This is how it was at the time until certain inhumane acts were made public, and the public included the Red Cross and other institutions. And then these institutions reacted by saying that this should be put to an end. This is when President Tudjman spoke out, including others, and they were saying that these camps need to be disbanded. I don't think that it was done. I don't know how long it took for the camps to be disbanded and cleared away. I can't tell you that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Tudjman, did he have any intelligence services forwarding to him information about what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, he was certainly informed, just as it was certain that the minister of defence was in daily contact with Boban and other leaders in Herceg-Bosna. I have no doubt concerning that, and I don't bring that into question at all. If that needs to be proven, then we should be able to prove these elements as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that you're trying to say that President Tudjman was informed about the existence of those camps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, I'm advised by Ms. Matacic, who does speak and read Croatian, that indeed in the book the word "concentration" does not appear, and I'm happy to have that corrected to that extent. However, I think the witness has made his position quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I could next ask you to move down the page or find where you see the words: "In the 12th of October, 1993, edition of Danas ..." At the bottom of page 262. It says: "... Manolic had the following to say about the responsibility of the Croatian authorities for the war with the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina: 'I expressed my disagreement with the Croatian policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina by taking a critical stance towards the steps that were taken in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna vis-a-vis the general interest of the Croatian people in BH. I believed, and I still do, that isolating the Herzegovinian Croats weakened the overall Croatian --'" I'm going to suggest that perhaps that word is "corpus. " What's been said is "corps" in English. "'-- in BH and the BH position in the resolution of the crisis as a whole.'" It's not -- at least in translation, sir, in the English, when it says isolating, "that isolating the Herzegovinian Croats weakened the overall Croatian" core, or corpus, what do you mean by "isolating the Herzegovinian Croats" in that context? And maybe it's a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not a translation error. Rather, this involves facts. The fact was, or the fact is, that Croats do not only live in Herzegovina. Rather, they live in all other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They're more numerous in some areas than in others, somewhere they constitute minority and somewhere they constitute majority. These are the people who felt most threatened when the conflict between Croats and Muslims broke out, because up until that time, more or less they resisted the Serbian aggression together. They resisted Karadzic together. And following this, their situation became unbearable, if I can put it that way. That was the greatest error Croatia committed in relation to Herceg-Bosna, its functioning, and the fact that it encroached upon the interests of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina to some extent. This is why when in one instance I mentioned Kljuic, I also say that there must be some room for the position that Kljuic had concerning that problem, to which President Tudjman said that he said that he was speaking from the shadow of Izetbegovic's influence. However, that wasn't true. That wasn't the case, no. He was simply voicing the thoughts of Croats who lived in certain areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina where they did not have majority. Those were the enclaves, such as Bosanska Posavina, that had this position, and the position of these people was amplified by Kljuic and, following that, his successor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you, sir, to go to page 265 of the book, to the first full paragraph on that page, 265. And for those looking at the English excerpt, top part of page 3 of this particular set. Sir, you here make reference to something you mentioned a few minutes ago. You have that. In reference to an interview that you gave to Globus on the 21st of January, 1994. This is not something you just said today, this is something you said apparently as far ago as January, 1994. It says: "Its title is indicating that: 'Mate Boban was calling Croats to move out of Bosnia collectively and go to the islands and to Istria!' It was without doubt that the most severe and the most radical critic of the official Croatian policy regarding the BiH - which particularly stressed the war between Croats and Muslims which culminated at that time." Can you provide the Judges with any additional information as to when it was that Mr. Boban called for people -- Croats to move out of Bosnia and how that, if you know, fit into any sort of policy at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that started with the Karadzic-Boban agreement. The portion of the agreement which steps aside from the ethnic principle of division within Bosnia-Herzegovina is the essence, is the starting point, if I can say so, of that policy which prompted Boban to make this appeal to these Croats, Croats from the Banja Luka region. It was mostly from that area that the Croats were moved out. That was the greatest tragedy that befell Croats due to this unrealistic policy pursued by Herzegovina lobby within Bosnia and Herzegovina. As a politician, I have to say -- I have to wonder what's going on. Is Bosnia and Herzegovina on the verge of a break-up? No. I was stating that it wasn't, that Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign state which existed in that territory within the AVNOJ borders, within the borders recognised by the UN, had to continue existing. And this is the case to this day even though it's been more than ten years since that time. As for internal tensions and internal partitions, I think that that will continue to exist for the next ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On this very point, sir, in the next paragraph of your book, you say, "In spite of all, I still think that Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot fall apart." Having said that, you then go to the next paragraph and you say: "I am also against talking about an 'expanded Croatia.' There should not be talking about Croatia expanding at the expense of the neighbouring state. That brings us into the position -- in the position of aggressor which, by use of force, wants to take the territory from the others." You said there should not be talk about this. Who was talking about an expanded Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two issues are important here. First of all, why am I saying here that Bosnia and Herzegovina cannot fall apart? Well, first of all, because the strongest ethnic group were the Muslims and they were in favour of that state. They were in favour of an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina. The second issue is also important and that is that it was international recognised, which made it more difficult to partition, and it made it more difficult to change the borders that others may have wanted to change in their own interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was it -- who were some of these people who wanted to change borders? You just said now "it made it more difficult to change the borders that others may have wanted to change." Who were the others?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we've already said that this whole group in Herceg-Bosna wanted to change those borders. We also have to add to this, if you recall, the fact that some 10 municipalities had asked the president for protection, and they wanted to be annexed to Croatia. So on the one hand we have a person who is threatened, who is looking for salvation in those small municipalities. They're looking for salvation by seeking the protection of their mother country, which is called Croatia. But the organisers of Herceg-Bosna, I think they wanted to do this consciously. And what the ultimate consequences would be, that's a question now. There were various kinds of ideas as to what should happen to this Herceg-Bosna, whether it would be annexed to Croatia or whether it would function as a kind of banana republic in the area. But later on, in the Washington Agreements, this led to the current situation, which I feel should be respected. But this cannot be done by those people who are the exponents of a war policy against the Muslims. People like Boban and the others who followed him who were the exponents of a war option cannot do this. This new policy can be waged only by those people who, even when there was an armed conflict with the Muslims, pointed out that there were other options, that agreements could be reached to protect all ethnic groups, whether Croats, Muslims, or Serbs. And I think that such people will come to the fore increasingly. President Tudjman replaced Boban. He told him it's not your fault. In other words, it's somebody else's fault. Whether he was referring to Susak or to himself, I don't know. We can't ask him that any more. But it's a fact that he replaced Mate Boban from the prominent position which carried the war option against the Muslims. This means that it was his assessment also that such a man could be a hindrance in the implementing of the Washington Agreements and co-existence with the Muslims. And what I said to him was don't replace just Boban. Replace everyone who was in favour of that. Not because we should take revenge on those people but because they are incapable of implementing the policy of the Washington Agreements, that is co-existence in a joint federation. The sooner we remove those people, the sooner we will gain the confidence of the Muslims who will then be able to accept cooperation. This doesn't mean that there were not those on the opposite side who were in favour of a war option and that Izetbegovic should not have carried out the same kind of thing on the other side, thereby creating the conditions for a more normal life in the federation, because look at what happened. When the Washington Agreements were formally accepted, the people in favour of the war option kept looking for obstacles, kept looking for reasons not to implement the Washington Agreements. They couldn't agree about who was going to be the chairperson somewhere, then they couldn't agree about the borders of certain cantons. All this was simply their disagreement with the newly arisen situation following the Washington Agreements. The state of Herceg-Bosna and its exponents formally accepted those agreements. I remember Prlic at this meeting while we discussed accepting the Washington Agreements, and in my view he approach the problem constructively, enumerating the points on which one should work in order to implement the Washington Agreements. But not everybody thought in the same way. They were thinking about how to complicate matters and how to not implement the agreements. And then what followed was the Dayton Accord, which was more radical in resolving the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you next to go to page 267 of your book, second paragraph. And for those following in the English excerpt, it is on page 4, the third paragraph on that page. And if you see that, sir, it's the paragraph starting: "The more frequent statements ..." It says: "The more frequent statements by the most responsible people about the military engagement of the Croatian army against Muslims 'in defence of Croatian people' are not realistic. Now that defence is relevant for Central Bosnia, and if it continues that way it will soon be relevant for the Neretva. Politics has to see all the consequences of possible military engagement on the territory of the other sovereign state. The world would see such an engagement as aggression of Croatia against internationally recognised state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We would get the same treatment as Serbia." Sir, can you tell the Judges what you know about the engagement of military forces of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina during this time and, in particular, in reference to 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a conflict there are various ways in which the conflict spreads. First of all, volunteers went, people who had been born there but who lived in Zagreb and other parts of Croatia or the world. This was justified both from the international viewpoint and from the viewpoint of these people who went into a conflict with the Muslims. However, it transpired, because of the strong Muslim potential, that the Croat forces experienced a crisis. They were pushed back. A Muslim woman said to me, "Just a little while longer and we'll push them into the sea." That was in late 1993, early 1994. Then the Croatian leadership, the president and Supreme Commander, was faced with a question of how to help to avoid a military disaster in Bosnia-Herzegovina. President Tudjman, in view of the constitutional solution that exists in Croatia which says that Croatia can use its army in another state only with the approval of the parliament had room for manoeuvre to try to find ways and means of helping the HVO forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were facing disaster, without coming into conflict with international policy which forbade engagement in another state. Our constitution also forbade it. Therefore, Croatia cannot be accused -- the Croatian state cannot be accused of participating in the war against the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because that's simply not correct. There was engagement. One can accuse the Supreme Commander. There is some evidence for that. As for the minister of defence, there is a lot of evidence about his involvement. But this was abuse of office. They were abusing their office in order to attain some goals which were not the goals of the Croatian state as a whole or the goals of its constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, let's be clear on this point, though. Apart from the legality under the Croatian constitution, it is your testimony that the president of the state, the minister of defence of the state, and other people, senior officials of the state, sent elements of the Croatian army into Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One should read the transcripts and see the words of President Tudjman and then one will see what his position was and how he defended it. He said quite clearly, "We cannot enter into a conflict with the international community by deploying the Croatian army, but we will help in every way, using every means." And it's well-known how assistance was provided to the HVO and Herceg-Bosna at that point in time. I think that assistance was given in this way, and that's what was most positive in this entire conflict. The position in which the HVO found itself in Bosnia-Herzegovina forced the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, and also President Tudjman and Gojko Susak, to seek solutions through negotiations, by peaceful means. And this led to the adoption of the Washington Agreement as the solution. The Washington Agreement had a very positive provision which said that the federation, or part of the federation, could enter into a -- not a coalition but a confederation with Croatia. All those sinners who had advocated the war option, who had wanted to accede to Croatia, to the mother country, they all found justification in this provision of the Washington Agreement, but it was never implemented. On the contrary, it is absent from the Dayton Accords because it would have caused far more fatal consequences. Not just in Bosnia-Herzegovina but also in Europe and the world, because worldwide there are problems with various ethnic groups and national groups living on other territories, in Hungary, Romanija, Spain, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, I would like to say something, if you allow me. I think you're mixing up a few things. The question which was put to you was this: In light of the difficulties experienced by the HVO, aid was provided, and on page 29, line 12, you answered that President Tudjman had said, "We cannot come into conflict -- we cannot have a conflict."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A legal conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And therefore, it was necessary to help the HVO in different ways. What I'm interested in is to know, before the Washington Agreement, how did Croatia help the HVO? Either you know or you don't know. If you don't know, you say you don't know. If you know, please tell us, and tell us what kind of information you had at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some information that I know personally. The issue of weapons, weapons came from Croatian depots through the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Funding of that group also went through certain channels. And when I say "channels," I'm not referring to legal channels. A legal channel would have been if in the budget of the State of Croatia there had been an item "Assistance to Herceg-Bosna," but that wasn't there. But still funds had to be supplied. This channel was the minister of finance and the Croatian banks, together with some prominent institutions or, rather, branch offices that the banks had in Herceg-Bosna. I think one should also say that accepting the Washington Agreement occurred after something we all remember that was said in the Security Council of the United Nations, and this was that elements of the Croatian army are in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This means that the United Nations and the Security Council had information on the basis of which they could say this. President Tudjman and the leadership of Herceg-Bosna were unable to deny it. I don't want to go any further into investigating this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you yourself personally in your position, did you know at the time that certain members of the Croatian army were in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legally, one didn't know it. It was kept secret. But there were illegal channels one could find out about. There were no documents about this. There are no such documents in existence. There were three stages: First, volunteers who had been born there; secondly, some parts of Special Purpose Units who were needed to strengthen the HVO were sent there. And when the Security Council discovered this, it must have had a lot of evidence to support such a statement, because it's well-known that there were thousands and thousands of intelligence agents in the area, all sorts of intelligence agents in various battalions - BritBat, the French Battalion - and they all sent intelligence about what was happening in the area. So that it was no secret to them, but it was a secret to our public and media. Not much was said about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At one point you said the minister of defence had, when you talked about Tudjman, had gone beyond his duties. Could you shed some light on this, please, and elaborate on what you have said a while ago; i.e., the position of the minister of defence when you talked about logistical support. You said aid was provided in different ways to the HVO. In what way had the minister of defence gone beyond what was expected of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. President Tudjman was the commander-in-chief of the army. The minister of defence was only part of the military sector. I think that very often there was some overlapping or adaptation. The minister of defence might do something that the president might not approve at a certain point in time. And this did happen. We can go into it if needed. So that the relationship between the Supreme Commander and the minister of defence, in formal terms, the minister of defence is appointed by the commander-in-chief, the president of the republic, so he should answer to him, he should be responsible to him. However, very often in my speeches I did not go for the president directly. I went for the minister of defence, because I felt him to be the operative agent of this disastrous policy. It was disastrous for the Croatian people. On the other hand, leaving open the possibility for the president to express his own views, but as we have seen, he did accept responsibility for the policy being implemented in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I can neither help him nor otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the name of the minister of defence? We need to have this in the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the minister of defence was Gojko Susak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, you asked him a direct question back on page 31, line 14, if he -- if he personally knew at the time. First I would like a clarification. What time are we speaking about? Secondly, what was his official position? Because if he knew, he was in the government, and again I point to the transcript and perhaps he may be again advised of his rights, because he's incriminating himself if indeed he was part of the government at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for the record, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. This kind of question can be asked during cross-examination. But as far as dates are concerned, at the time, what position did you hold? Were you a Member of Parliament? Were you in the Minister's cabinet? Were you advisor to the president? At the time you knew that aid was being provided, what was your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position was president or Speaker of the Upper House of the Croatian parliament, the House of Counties. This was not an operative office. I was presiding over that house of parliament where legislative activity was discussed. Therefore, I was not in direct contact with any operative matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From when to when, please, were you president of this Upper House? From when to when, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From March, 1993, to April, 1994. A year. That was the critical time we are now discussing. But I did participate in politics. Participating in politics through discussions, interviews, and so on is one thing, and direct decision-making on particular issues for which one is responsible is something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Mr. Praljak, because we need to take a break. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I wish to have a correction entered in the transcript. Mr. Manolic spoke out the name of the minister of defence, Gojko Susak as Susak. I think one should know the first and last name of the minister we're talking about so much. It's Susak, not Susak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Also, Mr. President, if we could ask whether he was a member of the security council at the time and whether he was participating in any discussions regarding -- where we have presidential transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the Christian name of the minister of defence, Mr. Manolic. What was the Christian name of the minister of defence, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minister of defence was called Gojko Susak. Gojko was his first name and Susak his last name. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Just one last question relating to what Mr. Karnavas has said. Were you a member of the security council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ex officio, as the Speaker of parliament, I was a member of that council, and one can see from the transcript what positions I advocated and what positions were advocated by others, including the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the president of the Upper House is automatically a security council member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, automatically. But still he has to be appointed by the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were appointed by the president, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. I was appointed by the president, as were all the other members of that Council for National Security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now 10.30. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have until 12.30. Please go ahead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before we go on to the next document and/or continue in your book, I should say, based on the questions the President has asked, let me go back to the issue of finances and funding. I think the question -- or the answer you gave was specifically in section with military assistance, in particular weapons. Can you provide to the Judges any information you have about how Herceg-Bosna and the HVO in general were funded or financed.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have direct information concerning that. I can only give you -- or, rather, the direct information can only be provided by the ministers of finance who held office in the Croatian government at the time, and perhaps some bankers through whom these transactions were implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Nonetheless, as a senior official of the Croatian government, did you have any understanding as to how such funding or financing was being provided?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only illegally. It is certain that one portion of it came from fundraising efforts outside of the country, that is to say Canada, Australia, and so on, but one portion of the aid was provided through Croatian finances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting, but the witness mentioned certain officials. Perhaps he could give us names. Say he said minister of finance or other persons that he implicated, could he give names, not just positions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you can find such information. Don't ask me for that. These are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, the problem lies in a fact that we are here in verbal proceedings, which is to say that what you say here needs to be supported by the documents. If you don't give us the name of the minister of finance, and if we don't have it in any document, then we may run into a problem. This is why Mr. Kovacic wanted you to give us some names which will be shown on the screen afterwards. Later on, when the Judges work on the judgement, then they can refer to the name of the minister of finance. If you remember the names of any ministers of finance, then please tell us. If you forgot this, then please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the names right now, even though I know all of the people who held that office in various Croatian cabinets throughout that time. But perhaps I would make a mistake if I were to give you a name now, so I'd rather refrain from giving any names. However, this is this is information that can easily be obtained. These are people who legally held offices, and the dates are well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you, and I apologise, but prior to that the witness mentioned some banks which took part in these operations. There are plenty of banks in Croatia. Could he give us the names of banks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that these transactions were realised through Privredna Banka --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the other name of the bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned two banks; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you assist us? The interpretation, I don't believe, got the name of the second bank. We've got Privredna Bank. Did you mention a second bank?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; Zagreb Bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And continuing on the matter of finances for a moment, did you ever obtain any information or do any calculations as to what it cost the Croatian government to support the HVO in the war against the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in one of my interviews I gave such an analysis which provided the figures at the time for the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the armed forces that were engaged in combat at the time. That was the basis. And I provided the figure at the time. I think it was 1 billion of dollars or something around that figure. This is how much the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina cost us -- or, rather, the HVO cost us that. I obtained this figure through the Ministry of Defence. Assistant minister for mobilisation had all the figures for military formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those of the HVO, not of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. [Interpretation] Once again, the same questions, Your Honour. The witness once again mentioned that he obtained this information through assistant minister for mobilisation within the Ministry of Defence. Can he give us the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Ademic [phoen] who was in charge of the lists within the ministry. At the same time, he was in charge of mobilisation of those who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina but were residing in Zagreb at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, is it Ademic or Ademnic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, I don't have all of my teeth so you can attribute this to that. It is Adanic. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] All right. So it is Adanic with an N and not Ademic with an M, and he was born in Varazdin, in Northern Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] And he was within a ministry in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be quite specific now and let me now be a pedant here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So it's Mr. Adanic. But please tell us this: You said that he was in charge of the list of Croatians born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. How did he obtain such a list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that it was some very accurate list, but this was information that was generally known. One would know that these people were from Herzegovina, that they hailed from there. At the time when we had the HVO crisis, when the HVO was under pressure from the enemy, the mobilisation was conducted in Zagreb and these people were asked to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina and to join the HVO. Some of them - I can't give you the exact figure - responded to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're trying to tell us that the mobilisation was carried out in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Zagreb and in Croatia as a whole, if we can say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can next ask you to go to page 281 of your book. And for those following in the English excerpts, it is the -- it is -- the next excerpt begins on the first page "11. Beginning of the Parliament Crisis." "11. Beginning of the Parliament Crisis." And again, Mr. Manolic, at page 281 of your book. Sir, did you call at some point for Mr. Susak to be either fired or that he should resign from the Croatian government, given everything you've told us about this morning?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that under normal circumstances, after all the defeats suffered by the HVO in Bosnia and Herzegovina it would have been normal for an architect or the main proponent of that policy to leave office. That was the point that I was making in my interview at the time. What it hinged on then was whether the president would support that or whether the president would replace Speaker of the parliament, or perhaps me, who at the time was the president of the Upper House, and the president opted for the second option, which led to the crisis that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So touching back on what we discussed yesterday, sir, what we may come to again toward the end of your testimony, there came a time essentially where you represented -- you represented one point of view and Mr. Susak represented the other point of view, and it was you that was forced out of the government?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not the government, rather, the commander-in-chief, President Tudjman. That's the difference. Because the government of Croatia -- rather, the cabinet did not really get involved with the problems of Herceg-Bosna at the time, no. They mostly focused on economic issues and other daily problems that cabinet had to deal with, and in that sense it was the commander-in-chief who was the decision-maker, and he implemented this through the minister of defence. Occasionally some other people would be involved in these matters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, continuing again on page 281 of your book, going down into the next paragraph, you seem to make a point of saying this was -- the conflict between you and Mr. Susak was not simply a personal conflict or a personality conflict, some might say, and it goes on to say: "Actually that was a conflict of two totally different and incompatible policies - one which was behind the instigating the war of Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the line of division of that internationally recognised state --" Would you like a drink of water? Are you okay?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel fine. This is just a type of cough that is typical for the elderly. Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I was reading from the next paragraph of your book, and: "... one was behind instigating the war of Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and on the line of division of that internationally recognised state and connecting of so-called Herceg-Bosna to the Republic of Croatia, and the other which from the beginning of the crisis in BiH insisted on complete territory of Bosnia and union of Croats and Muslims fighting against the aggression of greater -- Great Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Should we clarify something? I think it's high time we clarified something. When the Prosecutor refers to "your book," we need to clarify whether these comments uttered now by the Prosecutor, are they words of Mr. Manolic or the person who edited the book? Because we're not quite sure whether this is said in third person, whether these were the words uttered by Mr. Manolic or not. This is not a book that Mr. Manolic wrote. No. This is a book about Mr. Manolic. And we can see in one portion it says who edited this book containing the interviews of Mr. Manolic, so we need to clarify whether these are the words uttered by Mr. Manolic or by someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you're not right. These are the interviews that I gave, and they are accompanied by the comments of the person preparing the book or editing the book. And it is quite clear in the text which words should be attributed to the editor and which words should be attributed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you need to make it quite clear which words were uttered by the witness and which words represent the comments of editors or the person preparing this book. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- without reading the Croatian, I'm afraid -- I apologise to the Chamber, but without reading the Croatian I can't readily do that. I'll ask the witness to assist us in that regard, and I'm sure that if counsel thinks something is improper or misleading, I'm sure I'll be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that Mr. Kovacic is about to help you as well. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there is some additional information that might be helpful for you. I know that not the entire book was translated, rather, only portions of it, and it seems that this is a selection of various interviews provided by this witness throughout a period of time. So the context is quite important for each of these interviews, and generally we can't establish the temporal context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if I may reply to Mr. Kovacic. It is clear on the face of each interview when it was given, to which magazine and when, and I don't think that there's any confusion at all. The book is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may reply. I'm not doing this in order to confuse the witness. Mr. Manolic, what you said is quite true. We fully agree on this. However, it is not reflected in the transcript. So based on the transcript, one cannot tell what the witness is talking about, and we are interested in the transcript for the most part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, when you pose your questions, please try to clarify whether these were the words of the witness or not, and try to give us the date, because this witness seems to have a very good memory, and he should be able to help us with the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do -- I'll certainly do my best. Again, I have to say, and I apologise, but I -- since I do not speak the -- or read the Croatian language, it's a bit difficult, but I'll try to get the witness to assist us as much as possible. I would like to note for the record, Your Honour, what's been said. This is the book. It was published in 1995, and based on everything that was said yesterday in particular, I can hardly think that it was any surprise that this witness would come -- and this is well known; anybody can buy this in any book store -- at least, could at one time, any book store in Zagreb, and if these witnesses knew -- excuse me, these Defence teams knew since at least March, if not sooner, that this witness was coming, I'd be very surprised if most of them haven't bought this book a long time ago. Be that as it may, Your Honour, I'll do the best I can to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are quite grateful to Mr. Scott. I intervene precisely because we have read the book. I just looked at the transcript, and this portion that Mr. Scott attributed to the witness -- or, rather, I looked at the translation, and in the translation I was able to see that in the last portion it says that Manolic has uttered words against Mr. Susak. It is quite clear that this was edited by something -- someone, that these were not the words uttered by Mr. Manolic, and this is what my intervention pertained to, that we need to be clear whether the words were uttered by Mr. Manolic or the words are somebody else's comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, please try to make it clear whether something was stated by the witness or the person working with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you've heard the exchange and the statements of counsel in the last few minutes. As I direct you to various parts of your book, passage of the book that everyone in the courtroom knows about and probably has, if you can assist us, please, any points where -- what your words, what might be somebody else's words, or, please, if a certain position has been attributed to you, if you think it's not accurately stated, please say so. Can we agree to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we can agree. It is quite clear. There is text preceding each interview where we have the date, the magazine where the interview was published. Following that, there is a short comment by the publisher, and then there is the journalist's question to which I provide my reply. And while we still see the present screen, then let me say this: Yes, this was my response to those who were saying that this hinged on a personal conflict between myself and Mr. Susak as minister of defence. I said to all these people explicitly that this was no personal conflict. Rather, this was a conflict of two policies, and I believe that their policy was detrimental to the interests of Croatia as a state and Croatian people living in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe I was quite clear there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I'm trying to -- in light of what's been said this morning, I'm looking at some of the notes to see how we might gain some time without being too repetitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could go, sir -- sorry, I'll need some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist you? Perhaps I can help the Defence find their way in my book. If you take page 357. All of you should have that page. It says there published -- the interview was published in Novi List on the 14th of January, 1995. So this pertains to that period of time only. And then you can see in its entirety what I said, what my analysis of events was. I don't think that there should be any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go to page 287 of your book, page 287, second paragraph. And for those following in English, it is the third and last page of that particular excerpt, toward the bottom of the page. And, sir, I'll ask you this, and again I'll ask you if these are your words. There's a section on page that starts, and this goes back to something the President Judge Antonetti was asking about a few minutes ago. It says, "Even the lowest level spies dealing with Herceg-Bosna knew about the camps." Here again, the English says "concentration camps," I don't know if it's in your -- "... knew about the concentration camps from the first day they were set up. How could then Gojko Susak not have known? However, it is not about whether Gojko Susak knew about the concentration camps which indescribably damaged both the Croatian state and the Croatian national interest and which compromised Croats civilisationally, morally and politically as those partly responsible for the war in Bosnia. All that is past now and time should not be wasted on that. I want to ask now who made a political decision for the concentration camps to be set up in Herceg-Bosna? Further on, who made a decision for East Mostar to be under siege for many months? Who made or approved the decision for the old bridge to be destroyed? The bottom line consequence of all these questions is who decided that Croats should wage a war against Muslims?" Now, sir, first off, are those your -- are those your words? Excuse me.
