utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, entirely my words uttered during that period of time when I gave that interview, when I provided that analysis of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you specifically ever, sir, get any answers to those questions that you just stated here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Specific answers to this were never provided. I think that the tragedy is that it is this Tribunal which will have to provide answers to these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You go on in the next paragraph and you say, "Who, therefore, started the war against the Muslims?" The book goes on to say: "The one who started the war has to be held responsible. The fact is that Minister Susak was the one who was involved most of all in the implementation of the Croatian politics towards Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, are those your words, and if they're your words or if they're in somebody else's words -- they are your words?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, my words. No confusion there whatsoever. It is very easy to set aside, to distinguish the comment given by the editor of the book. My words are clearly published. There is no dilemma as to which were my words and which were the -- which are the added commentaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm looking just to get the page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going -- Mr. Manolic, if you could direct your attention to page 283 of your book, the second paragraph actually beginning on that page, page 283. And for those following in English, this is a separate now excerpt, Your Honour. It starts with -- the first words on the top of the page are, "The reply of President Tudjman ..." That's the first words of that particular excerpt. And if you have that, then I'm going over to the second page of the translation, to the first paragraph starting on the second page of the excerpt. And again, Mr. Manolic, I'm directing you to page 283, the second paragraph on that page. And as soon as I point this out to you, again I'll ask if these are your words. It says: "All those Croatian politicians who not so long ago claimed that the co-existence in the BiH was always a fake, a fake one, can be ashamed today of their statements because those statements were unfounded either in history or in the present BiH." Are those your words?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are entirely my words. This is my polemic with all those who sought a solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina in the war option; Karadzic, Mate Boban, and all the others who wanted to solve problems of the internal order of Bosnia and Herzegovina through weapons and war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say that they claimed that the co-existence in --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what follows is also important, because I'm always searching for solutions, for ways out of certain problems. The question to be answered is why people were getting killed. This had to be put to the politicians who accepted war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, although what was important now was to search for peaceful solutions, solutions that would be acceptable to everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina, all the groups there. I think I was quite clear referring to the situation that was developing on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say in the sentence that I referred you to, that "those who claimed that the co-existence in BiH was always a fake one," what do you mean by that? In what way was co-existence claimed to be fake?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in order to lead the people into a military confrontation, something had to be said about the history. They were denying that there had ever been co-existence on that territory, but it is a fact that throughout the 40 years of Tito's Yugoslavia there had been peace among all three ethnic groups which were now in an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct -- sorry. If I can direct your attention, Mr. Manolic, to page 284 of your book, to the third -- the fourth paragraph on that page. Page 284, the fourth paragraph. And to -- in the English excerpt, it is the last page of the -- about the middle page [sic] of the last page of that particular excerpt. And again we come back to the issue of the Croatian army participating in Bosnia. Do you see this language, please: "The international community was constantly warning us. A year ago our leadership was told not to interfere in Bosnia with our logistics and our influence. Finally, the entire international community stood up concerning the problems around the Croatian involvement in BiH. The UN was informed earlier but the statement that 'the elements of the Croatian army participate in the war in Bosnia' was issued only at the intervention of the representatives of the BiH government in the UN. This was the final warning which would have been definitely followed by sanctions for the participation in war against the Muslims." Can you tell the Judges generally what role in the politics or the policy of the Croatian government at this time, or at least of Tudjman and Susak, did the threat of sanctions by the international community play, or the UN or other international bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that President Tudjman, as the Supreme Commander, found himself hit by this threat from the Security Council and that this was one of the important elements that led to the acceptance of the Washington Agreement without any objections, because further conflicts would certainly have brought sanctions down upon Croatia. It would have been isolated in the world, and this would have brought into question the sovereignty that Croatia had gained, which was ultimately the goal of President Tudjman, myself, and all the rest of us who had participated in the turnaround in the 1990s in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If -- I believe that concludes the material in your book, at least for the Prosecution. If I could ask the registry to please now display for you Exhibit P 09645.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And of course -- do you have -- yes. Can the witness be shown that in Croatian, please? It's there. It looks like we just have it flipped around, because we have both versions on our screens. Thank you very much. Sir, if you have that, as just a particular example of the type -- the interviews and articles that you gave around this time, this appears to be an article dated the 1st of April, 1994. And directing your attention to about the middle of that page: "According to Manolic, the vital difference between him and Tudjman lies in the strategic policy regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as the Washington Agreement is concerned, I believe that my option for Bosnia prevailed. It is based on cooperation between Croats and Muslims and on respect for the integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina." The first question, are those your words when you say "As far as the Washington Agreement is concerned, I believe that my option prevailed"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic, I hadn't seen you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Exhibit 9645 is not the original interview published in Globus. It is a -- an article by Tanjug, a Belgrade newspaper agency, which summarises the interview given by the witness, which is allegedly published in Globus. We do not have the original text of the interview in Globus, so we are unable to check how accurate the summary is. The summary was made by a Serbian news agency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, please bear this comment in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, without -- let me just ask you, does this state for us now, this statement where it says - again, the one that I've read to you - does that accurately state your assessment of the situation that as far as the Washington Agreement is concerned, you believe that your option for Bosnia is the one that actually ultimately prevailed, at least up to the time of Washington?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my interpretation at that point in time, and you can see that the date of this news item is the 1st of April, which was when my intervention was actually taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the record, 1st of April, 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask the registry to next go to Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the period when the parliamentary crisis broke in the Croatian parliament, and the crisis was a result of the lack of agreement between my policy and the policy of Mr. Mesic and others who disagreed with the policy in question. This was a parliamentary crisis, and the president demanded that Mr. Mesic, the speaker of parliament, be replaced and that I be replaced from my office of Speaker of the House of Counties. The parliamentary opposition parties almost all took our side. The exception was the HSP. All the other opposition parties supported us, and this gave rise to the parliamentary crisis. President Mesic, just like me, had support among members of parliament in both houses, so that it was not a simple matter to resolve, and it was resolved with an agreement made among all the opposition parties and the ruling party headed by President Tudjman. The result was that President Mesic resigned in the House of Deputies and I resigned or, rather, was dismissed from the House of Counties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And now if I could -- thank you for that. If I could ask the registry to please display Exhibit P 09649. Sir, this appears to be again an interview with you in Globus dated the 6th of May, 1994; is that correct? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. This is already the period when I was no longer the president of the House of Counties and President Mesic was no longer the president of parliament, or the Speaker of parliament. This was the period when we founded a separate political party, the Croatian Independent Democrats. We were the opposition to the HDZ and the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you -- it's a fairly long interview, and if I could ask you to go approximately four or five pages into the document, I'm not quite sure where we'll be in the Croatian version, but it will be well into the document. If you can find the point where Mr. Butkovic asked you this question: "Can you estimate how much money Croatia spent on the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?" And it's the next to the last page of the English version for those looking at the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to draw the Court's attention to the fact that we are again talking about snippets from the alleged interview. I think we should be provided with the context. You cannot extract a single sentence. It's not realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in this particular document, you may see from the English version, it's pretty apparent, that the first four or five pages of the document has to do with the -- or at least the first several pages I'm looking at it again now, the adoption of the kuna or -- as currency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think anyone in the courtroom's going to suggest that that's an issue in the courtroom or relevant to this case at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, if you can find the place where the question was put to you, "Can you estimate how much money Croatia spent on the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?" And I asked you this earlier. You made reference to the fact that you had at one point looked into this and had some information. I think you said it was given in an interview. If you look at these -- your answer, two paragraphs here, is that consistent with the information that you received and provided in the interview in May, 1994? That is in the second paragraph, it's estimated that: "All together, the war with the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina cost the Republic of Croatia at least 3 million Deutschmarks a day! Since the war lasted nearly one year, it can be estimated that the war cost us a total of nearly 1 billion Deutschmarks." Do you see that? It's on the second page of the Croatian-language version, if that assists you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What matters is whether I remember it, not whether I found it. The analysis was not done on the basis of exact indicators. It was simply a calculation which is based on the expense of the war. That's what I'm talking about. And it follows on from the analysis I made previously in another interview. Butkovic is now posing the question again, and I cannot tell him the precise figure, just as I cannot tell you the precise figure now. One has to calculate this based on evidence, using financial experts to arrive at a realistic figure as to how much that war cost us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that -- that -- I'm not crossing the witness, but I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to cross the witness but I think it would be prudent if the Prosecutor would immediately ask clarification to what soldiers the witness is referring when he is mentioning 63 or 64.000 of soldiers. What, fighting in Croatia or in Bosnia? Whose soldiers? It is not visible from the article, at least from this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just double-check if I can see the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The article refers to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, it refers to the numbers of the HVO at that point in time. The HVO. Not the Croatian army; the other parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it doesn't change anything. Don't hold me to 3 billion or 2 billion. It doesn't really matter. Whether a subtle financial analysis would yield a figure of 2 billion or 3 billion, it doesn't really change things because the war brought with it financial sacrifices, human sacrifices, sacrifice of human lives, and all other kinds of sacrifices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just so the record is clear, then, you were talking about the cost to support the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that these are the costs to the government of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the essence. How else? They couldn't use the rocks of Herzegovina to create that kind of funding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I would like to ask Mr. Manolic not to insult the Herzegovinians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not insulting anyone. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Please put forward the facts. And what we could get from the rocks of Herzegovina, that's insulting and offensive, and please leave that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the registry to please show to the witness Exhibit P 00134. And, Your Honours, as we mentioned yesterday, we're prepared to provide a hard copy to the -- this is going to be the -- one of the presidential records, and if it's easier for the witness to follow in hard copy, we're prepared to give him one, with the Court's permission. May we, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, we're going to hand you a hard copy of the following transcript. It's up to you whichever you find to be the most useful, but I think you'd mentioned yesterday at one point, I think, that you thought it might be helpful to have the document.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would be best assisted if the text were on the monitor, if possible. If not, then I will search for it, but you know what it means to look for something in a hundred pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Manolic, in fact. All right. We'll proceed on the basis of what's on the screen, then, and if at some point you think you need to look at something in the hard copy, it will be available to you. If you have the first page of that exhibit, then, sir. Just as a reference point, do you see that this is a record of the meeting of the Croatian Democratic Union Presidency, held at a particular location on the 10th of March, 1992, chaired by Franjo Tudjman? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. I see it. I don't see the documents, though. It just says chaired by the president, Stipe Mesic away. Zdenka Babic, apologies. So this is who is absent. Perincic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. I was just going to direct you to some specific pages, but in terms of -- before we leave this first page, is it correct, sir, that in addition to Franjo Tudjman being the president of the Republic of Croatia, he was also the president of the HDZ political party in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's common knowledge. Throughout this period he was the president of the HDZ, until he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the first page, when it continues on, there's a reference to Boban. It says: "Mate Boban, vice-president from Bosnia-Herzegovina -" or at least BH - "is with us, since he is in Zagreb and since we have on the agenda, you have been given the agenda." Then if I can direct your attention to the third page, to the registry's assistance, the third page. And as far as I know, the third page in the English version the third page of the B/C/S version should be the same. They're discussing apparently agenda items and then it says, "No. So then the question of the BH HDZ leadership." And Boban says, "There's the president's resignation. There's the dual information system, and then indisputably bypassing the HDZ." And Tudjman says: "All right, the problem of the BH HDZ leadership." Now, is this a reference -- this is again dated the 10th of March, 1992. When it says the president's resignation, is that a reference to Stjepan Kljuic's resignation from the Bosnian party?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a discussion about the party, and Mate says that the president of the party, Mr. Kljuic, is resigning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can then direct everyone's attention well into the document, page 95 of both the original and the English version. Page 95. And one of the reasons, Your Honour, the document's been prepared this way is that indeed so we can establish the page correspondence so that the pages with numbers stay the same. That's one of the reasons we have so many pages, blank pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have page 95, sir, and then it says Mr. -- the president --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may suggest that the Prosecutor would refer to ERN numbers. Because I don't know whether you have seen the Croatian copy, Your Honour, but I would like to inform you that actually the pagination system which -- which those people in Tudjman's offices used is very suspectable, and sometimes one cannot control whether there are all the pages or not. So the only way to enable other people in the courtroom to know where to go is to use ERN numbers. I would appreciate it very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Scott, please give us the page number in Croatian and also page number of the translation. That's quite easy. You said that the English page is 95. That's the translation. Please give us the page number in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It appears to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It appears to be -- if you want the ERN number, it is 01508959, which is displayed on the screen. If counsel will open up their e-court system, they will find -- and open and follow that document, you will find that page 95 of the English version and page 95 of the B/C/S version are the same. We have it open now, and we have both versions on the screen, and they're both the same, but that is only if they will open up their e-court system and use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, if you have the page, the president's talking and then he refers to Boban -- if we can go up on the page, please -- or go down on the page. It's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour, we're having obviously some technical problems. Just to assist us, can the registry again show the very bottom of this page, the one that's being -- okay. Thank you. Apparently, Your Honour, for whatever reason, they're different paginations in different versions, because on one screen that we have open the page is exactly the same, word-for-word, and the one that's on the courtroom screen now it's not the same, so I don't know. We were trying to do that in fact to assist everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance. The English version, Your Honour, 95 starts on the last -- the last part of the page that was designated by Mr. Scott. At the very end you'll see. And it goes on to the following page, which would be 01508960 for my colleagues looking in the Croatian version. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I appreciate that. Let's see if we can get it sorted out. If you see that language, sir, where it says -- we'll have to -- can you go to the next page, then, in what's on the computer -- the courtroom screen in the Croatian, can you go to the next page, please. Keep going. Down, please. I'm told that it's page 99 in the B/C/S version, Your Honour. It's page 99 on the -- in terms of the images on the screen, it would be page 99. If that doesn't work, then we'll have to go to the hard copy, I guess. Can we -- can you further go down to the bottom of the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be simpler to put the B/C/S version on the ELMO. Then you can go ahead with your question and then the witness would either confirm it or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can do that for the time being, Your Honour, and see if we can sort it out. I apologise. We have been trying to avoid this problem, but apparently we haven't got all the bugs worked out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist you? The pages that you are going through now have nothing to do with -- with this process, because this deals with intra-party issues, tasks, who is to do what, and I believe that this is completely irrelevant to the proceedings here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me show you -- let me direct you to the section, sir, and we can see if it is or not. Could you just confirm that, for instance, Mr. Tudjman is both the president of the state and president of the party at the same time. So if you can see the part where he says: "Mate can inform us briefly. However, as you know, events have unfolded in the BH HDZ in such a way -" and going to the next page - "that Stjepan Kljuic, who - after the mistake with Perinovic - was excellent for that, who managed the election campaign brilliantly, but afterwards, recently, practically disappeared under Alija Izetbegovic's fez and the HDZ practically stopped leading an independent Croatian policy, our policy. This went so far that, just as Alija said that the war in Croatia was not his war, so Stjepan Kljuic told foreign newspapers - I do not know whether he did it here, too - but people told me that he said that we had ourselves to blame for this situation, for the war." And, sir, does this reflect the continuing -- what you've told us all morning so far is the dispute between these different factions, and is this a further reflection of that same dispute, at this particular instance involving Mr. Kljuic? That is, is Mr. Kljuic being one who is not for the Susak-Boban policy?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this has already been proven, namely that that was the reason. Kljuic did not want to implement the policy which led to the conflict with Muslims. He adhered to the position taken at the referendum where Bosnia and Herzegovina was established as a sovereign, integral state, Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the essence of the split that they had. What you are now mentioning, I don't see that on the screen, the reference of Mr. Izetbegovic. I think that his statement was incorrectly quoted, namely his statement about this not being our war. This was incorrect, because the rest of that sentence reads: "Our sons should not apply to the Yugoslav army." This is the key point. I think that this lack of accuracy when it comes to Izetbegovic's statement is something that needs to be corrected, regardless of who is to blame for the wrong interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, you anticipated my question in that regard exactly. The Judges have heard various references made in the trial so far to the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic at some point said something to the effect of, "This is not our war." Now, with that in mind, again, I know you just said this but perhaps you can say it a bit even more clearly and amplify on it, what was the actual context in which President Izetbegovic made the statement "This is not our war"? What was the actual context, and what was the full statement that President Tudjman [sic] made, not just the part that's been taken out of context?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not the statement of President Tudjman, rather, that of President Izetbegovic. I think that those who in a way blamed the Muslims for the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina frequently tend to quote this sentence of President Izetbegovic as the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I say that this quotation is incorrect because they failed to mention the rest of that sentence, because he spoke in the context of not sending people from Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Yugoslav People's Army. He wanted them not to respond to the call-up papers. That was the essence of what he was saying. It wasn't meant to represent that he was opposed to the Croatian thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like for Mr. Izetbegovic's title to be clarified. He's being referred to as president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No. He was the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he was the first among equals. There were seven of them elected by three peoples to represent them within that body. This is quite different from the title of president of a state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is true. This reflects the reality. This reflects the constitutional position held by President Izetbegovic. But ultimately, this makes no difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Manolic, you said something to us which will be further interpreted by the Judges. You said that when Mr. Izetbegovic said, "This is not our war," this sentence needed to be put in the proper context, because he also said within that context that the residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina should not join the Yugoslav army and that that was the gist of what he was saying. These words, "This is not our war," were uttered by him because he did not wish for the soldiers from Bosnia and Herzegovina to be mobilised into that army. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, it was the enemy army. That's what you need to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to clarify, just to continue on that for a moment, sir. When you say "the enemy army," this was the JNA, this was the army of Milosevic and the Serbs that was conducting various operations around this time. I don't have a specific operation in mind at the moment, but was conducting operations in Bosnia, in Croatia, and what Mr. Izetbegovic was saying was people from Bosnia should not go and join the JNA in its aggressive war against either Croatia or Bosnia or elsewhere, I suppose Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the public is sufficiently informed about the position of the Yugoslav People's Army from 1990 until it fell apart entirely in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, it is not the public who needs to be informed. Rather, it's the Judges. The Judges need to be informed. Therefore, please answer the question. Please clarify for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslav People's Army, which was created in Tito's period and developed over 40 years, was created in a context where people living in Yugoslavia were equal and it fully represented all of them. However, with the disappearance of Tito and the emergence of chaos in Tito's Yugoslavia, chaos prompted by the policy of Milosevic, this army gradually was transformed into Milosevic's army, regardless of the formal state of affairs where it was responsible to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, whose member Stipe Mesic was until a certain date in 1991. Following that period, that army fully aligned itself with Milosevic. It became an aggressor's army even though it was an aggressor's army even prior to that because it assisted certain Chetnik formations in instigating Serbian rebellion in Croatia. In many instances where our police went to intervene to protect the people, the army would step in as a buffer, as a buffer force between the rebels and our regular Croatian police forces. But whenever the enemy was under pressure, whenever the Chetniks or the rebel Serbs were under pressure, the army would step in and would, in a way, protect them. This is why from the very beginning we treated that army as an aggressor's army which fought against the sovereignty of Croatia. The army played the same role in Bosnia. I hope that I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You may continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can go -- if we can go to page -- I've been told that hopefully this will work. On the screen, if you go to page 105 of the B/C/S version, it should correspond to page 101 -- 105 of the English on the screen and 105 in the Croatian, I'm told, again are the same.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you need to clarify that these were the words of Mr. Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to ask you that. If you go back --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is not clear on its face.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. And that's one of the difficulties, of course, of being able to -- just pulling up one page at the time. You can't see that entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour will see from the English version page 99 that Mr. Mate Boban starts speaking and he continues speaking for several pages, and on page -- what I understand would be page 101 of your version, Your Honours, we'll try to -- yes. We'll try to straighten this out, but I don't think it will be possible in the time allowing for direct examination. But on page 101, it says: "Luckily, we had a man for financial affairs in the Ministry of the Interior, Bruno Stojic, a devoted man whom they wanted to dismiss in writing because of this, and this man has given us so far in our territory of Herceg-Bosna over 150 new Golf cars, not to mention the weapons, but I can say it because this is -- this is the party."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you provide any additional information to the Judges, Mr. Manolic, on Mr. Stojic's role in providing 150 new Golf cars and apparently weapons to the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before -- I'm sorry. May I? Before the witness answers that question, would Mr. Scott kindly clarify it so that we know the source of the witness's knowledge, whether he's speaking from personal information or whether it's a matter of speculation derived from whatever Mr. Boban may have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, you were in this meeting, and I'm just asking you, based on what's said here or based on any other conversation you had with Mr. Boban or heard Mr. Boban say around this time, can you provide any additional information about this information attributed or concerning Mr. Stojic? If the answer is no, you cannot, then just say so.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a session of the HDZ to which Boban was invited as the leading man of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I attended that session as well, so, yes, I heard the words of Mr. Boban personally when he presented a number of accusations against Kljuic and when weaponry and personnel appointments were discussed. However, these were all intra-party affairs and settling of accounts in order to get rid of Kljuic, in order to eliminate him, in a way, from the Presidency and leadership of the party so that one of those other people who would be passionately implementing the central policy could be appointed to that position, this policy that was in fact supporting the conflict with the Muslims, and this is something that Kljuic was against. As for these Golf vehicles and these words, "reliable men," I don't know him at all, I don't know the man, so I can't tell you whether he was talented in financial affairs or not. These are the words uttered by Mr. Boban. How he came up with this figure of 150 Golfs, I don't know. I think it needs to be clarified among these people, among these people who at that time lived in that area and worked there. At the session itself, it was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are confirming to us that Mr. Boban raised this issue of 150 Golfs, but on the other hand, you don't know Mr. Stojic personally, or you didn't know him at the time. So as for the number of 150, you know nothing about it except for what you heard from Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the figure I heard then. Nobody gave any comments at the session as to the origin or purpose or anything of the sort. No comments were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 150 cars which were obviously new needed to be purchased. A Golf is an expensive car. Was it the party who funded this purchase? And, if so, how could they have placed it at the disposal of somebody from the HVO, for example, or any other institution unless it was procured in this way? Who financed this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can tell you is what I heard at this session, I heard with my own ears, and I can tell you that there was no further comment concerning these 150 Golfs. We can only speculate. In Sarajevo there was a plant manufacturing Golf vehicles, so we can perhaps speculate that this was taken from the factory lot in Sarajevo. Now, as to whether somebody paid for them or didn't, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Could we go then, please, to page -- I'm told in the electronic English version and in the Croatian version it would be page 108. However, for those using the earlier distributed hard copy in the courtroom, in the English it will be page 104. So if you're using the electronic screens, it should be page 108 for both English and Croatian. If you're using the hard copy that was distributed yesterday, it will be page 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that page, sir, there's a reference, if you have it -- I don't know. Are we there? Okay. Yes. Sorry. You see a reference there to Gagro. The sentence, the particular passage, says: "However, among them, the main organiser and present there, was the general secretary of the HDZ. The president of Mostar municipality, the brother of this Gagro, et cetera." Did you know or know of a man named Gagro who was the president of the Mostar municipality at this time, as of at least March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that man. I know his brother who was our ambassador to France. I don't know what happened to him afterwards. I had no contact with this man, so I can't tell you anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know of his brother, the president of Mostar? Whether you knew him personally, did you know of him and his political stance at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would amount to speculation if I said anything further about Gagro. I think that there are people who can give you much more accurate information, who have direct knowledge of the fate of Gagro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If I can ask you to go -- to be shown page 110. Again on the electronic -- electronically, it will be page 110. For those using the English hard copy, it will be page 106. Toward the bottom of the page, I believe. Thank you. This is a man named Juric, Perica Juric. Perhaps you can tell the Judges who Juric was at this time and what his position, if any, was as of March, 1992, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perica Juric was one of the founders of the Croatian Democratic Union in Croatia, and throughout this period, 1990 and 1991, he was in a way in charge of contacts with the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that's how he came to know a large number of people in the Bosnia-Herzegovina milieu. I think he was very involved with respect to those eight municipalities in Bosanska Posavina where his contacts were intensive, we can say, and the standpoints he arrived at in his contacts with those people in that area, he conveyed to me and to President Tudjman, and he joined in all the discussions. He remained in the HDZ until we left in April, 1994, left the HDZ, and he also joined Mesic's newly founded party, the Croatian Independent Democrats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you could just then go then back to the passage where it says, "I would be so free as to propose -" this is Mr. Juric talking - "along with the presidents of the Croatian communities, Mr. Boban, Mr. Stanic, Mr. Barac, that is, the presidents of the communities, also Dr. Miljenko Brkic." Is Mr. Brkic, was he the one who became acting president of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina after Mr. Kljuic resigned?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They -- the top of the Croatian Democratic Union counted on Mr. Brkic as a person who could unite the Croatian corpus in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not just the Herzegovinians but the rest of the Croatian population who were not living in Herzegovina, but all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is why we decided that Miljenko Brkic could be the person to link up the overall Croatian interests in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was an eminent, respectable person in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think he is still held in high regard there. He disagreed with the policy inaugurated by Boban, so he, too, was left out of the leadership when Mate Boban took over the duty of president, or the office of president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we continue over on this passage onto the next page, which will be apparently 111 on the screen and 107 in the English hard copy. Mr. Juric is still speaking, and he says: "I think that this is very important and that together with our three top men the two of them will also ensure this component in our policy. The choice of an acting president is certainly your affair. You shall judge what is the next step to take regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina and, therefore, which of these men you can count on. This is purely operations, operational work which they will have to carry out in politics. Thank you very much. "The President: Does anybody wish to speak?" My question to you about this passage, Mr. Manolic, is why was it that the selection of the president in Bosnia-Herzegovina, why was that a matter for Franjo Tudjman to decide?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to go back again to the genesis of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was created with the direct support of the HDZ in Croatia. All changes, including formal changes, changes in the statute and platform, were made in cooperation between Croatia and part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is why Gojko Susak said at one point the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina is merely a branch of the Croatian Democratic Union of Croatia. When we say that, merely a branch, then it becomes evident that the overall policy was subject to control and inauguration in the branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to end my questions with this particular transcript there, Your Honours, and suggest this might be the time to take the lunch recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to what you've just said, does this mean that you share Mr. Susak's view on the fact that the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina is only a branch of the HDZ in Croatia, in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I never shared that entirely, that idea, but with respect to assistance in establishing the party, I know that people from Croatia, who lived in Croatia, participated in the founding Assembly, the constituent Assembly of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that they were later on involved in the work of the HDZ of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it's just about time to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I know, Your Honour. If I could just possibly try to clarify this before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this may be similar to an issue we may have been having yesterday. If I could just ask -- if I could just try to clarify the President's question, or your answer. When you say it was your view, are you telling us that it was your view that the party in Bosnia should not be the same as the HDZ party --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He should ask him what his view is. What is his view, as opposed to giving him a leading question. What is his view? He can state it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He said, Your Honour, he said at line 10 of page 72, "I never shared that entirely." He didn't say -- that's why I'm asking him to clarify. He said his view is that it wasn't, or that it shouldn't be, and that's my clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could you please make your point of view clear. You said you have never shared Susak's views on a number of subjects, and particularly as far as the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never entirely accepted that standpoint, and it's not contained in the documents of the statute or the platform, that it's a branch of the HDZ, but in the manner he wanted to influence the work of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he used that expression. My personal opinion is that in a sovereign state, regardless of whether its name is the same as the name of a party in a different state, one party must not impose its policies on another. There can be communication between equal entities on certain questions and issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas. You're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we want a clear and unequivocal statement from the gentleman. He says "not entirely." We're speaking in codes here, very nuancing codes that one would find perhaps in certain political systems. I would like to know what part. If he says, "I never entirely accepted," what part did he accept? So let's be clear and unequivocal. What part did he accept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This part which you accepted and a large part which you dismissed relating to the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the fact of the matter was that one had to respect, and in formal and in legal terms it was respected. I don't have the statute of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina with me, but it was never treated as a branch of the central HDZ, and I agree with this, that it was not a branch of the central HDZ, that it was an independent organisation bearing the same name based on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and active there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall stop there. It's past 12.30. We will have an hour and a half break, and we shall reconvene at 2.00. According to my calculations - but the registrar will have to confirm this - I think the Prosecution has so far used more than four hours. Theoretically, you should have two hours left, no more, no less. Mr. Registrar, could you give me the exactly calculation, please. We shall reconvene again at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing has resumed. The registrar calculated the time. The Prosecution has had four hours and three minutes, so the Prosecution has two hours left. The Bench, the Defence counsel, and Mr. Praljak have taken up one hour. So in future, I will speak less and not infringe on the time of the Prosecution or of the Defence. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would -- we certainly do not invite the Judges to speak less, because obviously many times the Judges' questions are the best questions, so we hope the Judges will inquire however you see fit to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, if I could ask the usher to please show you Exhibit P 00312. Exhibit 312. And if you have that, sir, if I could ask you again if we can just start by looking at the first page. This appears to be a record of a meeting, or at the top refers to a trip between the 4th and the 12th of July, 1992, and then specifically the third passage down talks about a meeting: "Mr. Tudjman received us for talks in a villa an on the 5th of July, 1992." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This makes a reference to a Mr. Brkic being present at this meeting, and do you recall that this is the Mr. Brkic who was in fact named the acting president of the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina following Mr. Kljuic's resignation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same Brkic. And this is his authentic report which I saw at the time when he was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the registry to go to page 3 of the document on the e-court, I believe. No. Yes, page 3 in e-court. For those following in English - and I'll explain why this is the case - it is the first -- first page 2. And the reason why there are multiple pages, two page 1s, two page 2s, Your Honours, is the original document was typed in a very small font which was not followed in the translation, so there are more pages in the translation than there are in the B/C/S original. So they were -- everything that was on page 1 of the Croatian version was still page numbered 1, and that's the reason. But -- so now I'm directing the courtroom's attention to the first page 2. In e-court it is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Starting at the top of the page, and if anyone wants to look back several pages previously, this is President Tudjman speaking. President Tudjman says: "The bringing of King Aleksandar, Mr. Panic, and others means that we must be sensible with respect to Croatia's policy in BH. We must not allow ourselves to be provoked because that's precisely what the enemy wants. We will continue to demand a cantonal arrangement in the areas, in those areas we have defended, where you need to introduce and organise your authority, and you must defend those areas firmly and prevent conflicts with the Muslims. That's not easy, but it is possible with the wise participation of all factors. Now I want to open up a discussion on the continued implementation of Croatian policy in BH." Mr. Brkic says -- he thanks President Tudjman for inviting them. Skipping down a couple of lines, Mr. Brkic says: "Many people are asking if the work of the party has been suspended or not, especially after events in Bugojno and elsewhere. The question is whether a convention should be held or not. What is Herceg-Bosna? What kind of association is it? And the Posavina and Central Bosnia also need to be clarified. What is their relationship with the state as a whole? What is the HVO? This has not been clarified sufficiently. HVO has suspended regular civilian authority and even the HDZ." Sir, in looking at that, you told us yesterday and today about some of your concerns in -- I think this morning you said setting up of a state within a state, and can you tell us whether what Mr. Brkic -- the concerns that Mr. Brkic is indicating or reporting here are that types of things that also concerned you about what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This report submitted by Brkic concerns the continuation of the conflict with Mr. Boban or, rather, with his policy. Brkic had a more liberal, more open policy of cooperation with the Muslims in mutual communication with a view to solving numerous problems. That's why Boban was -- was irritated by Mr. Brkic's speech and the policy he advocated. I think that I shared the standpoint of Mr. Brkic and supported him in his standpoints. Brkic is complaining about the violence perpetrated by Boban towards certain cadres in their tasks and the positions they were given and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can then direct your attention to the top of the second page 2, or page 4 in the electronic -- in the e-court version. Mr. Brkic is continuing on, and he says: "The HDZ party has adopted conclusions and paid tribute to the HVO for what it has done so far, especially regarding free territories. However, the HDZ does not agree with the suspension of civilian authority. I'm not saying that the HVO should not establish interim authority in some municipalities, especially in those places where there is no authority, but one has to be very careful in consideration of that. By establishing an office in Herceg-Bosna, it provokes a reaction and dilemmas about dual authority and which authority should be obeyed." Excuse me one moment. Forgive me, sir. Going back, directing your attention back to the previous page, Mr. Brkic. Mr. Brkic says -- at one point he says: "The HVO has suspended regular civilian authority and even the HDZ." And the question I was really looking for, I'm sorry, was: Did it come to your attention and was there a time when essentially the HDZ party, the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, became essentially suspended or defunct, largely defunct during the time of the conflict between the Croats and Muslims and it being replaced by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't go any further from what Mr. Brkic said, because he was in direct contact in the solving of the problems arising in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I could only support him and agree with him, but I cannot comment in detail as to what was going on in the area. I think Mr. Brkic would be able to describe this in much greater detail and more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, you mentioned a moment ago -- you said that Mr. -- I think you said that Mr. Boban became irritated about the meeting or the comments by Mr. Brkic. Can I ask you to look at the top of page 3 -- the first page 3 of the hard copy. And it's page 5 of the e-court versions. And it says, according to Mr. Boban, or Mr. M. Boban: "If I had known that these would be the participants in the meeting and that we would have this kind of a discussion, it is certain that I would not have come because I have far more pressing business." And is that what you're referring to when you say that Mr. Boban was irritated by the issues that Mr. Brkic was raising?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Boban couldn't bear criticism. Mr. Brkic's speech was critical of the existing situation which had been imposed by Boban, in a way, in the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he specifies the points on which he's critical. I think this is a very significant document, that it throws light on the events at the time. So this is all taking place in July, 1992. It's dated the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I then direct your attention to the next page, the second page 3 in the English hard copy, and page 6 in the e-court versions, both Croatian and English in the e-court. About the middle of that page, sir, if you can see, there are some statements or comments attributed to someone named Baric, Mr. V. Baric. Do you remember -- can you tell the Judges, do you recall who Mr. Baric was and any position he held at this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the gentleman, and I have no recollection of the name or anything associated with it. I think one could clarify this with people who were directly involved in the events.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would you -- looking just at Mr. Baric's comments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, is it Baric or Barac?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you're right, Your Honour, I think it's Barac. I probably mispronounced it. Perhaps the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you say Barac, Mr. Manolic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's Barac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking just at the content of Mr. Barac's comment, would you agree that he too was also expressing concerns about the HVO taking over authority in various places?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Brkic's way of thinking and his positions were not isolated. They were simply a reflection of what a broad circle of HDZ people in Bosnia-Herzegovina thought. So this meeting was held to clarify issues and see who was right; whether Brkic and the people advocating his positions were right, or whether Boban was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just to finish with this document, then, just so that the statement's in the transcript, what Barac said was: "I think that the very establishment of the HVO was a good thing but in those places in which the Muslims are a majority they do not recognise this because this is a quiet taking over of power. The policy of appointing senior personnel in Zenica is very bad. Almost all ranking officials are Muslims. Relations with other ethnic groups are very poor. There are warnings that a confrontation will occur." I think we can go on, then, to the next -- if I could ask that the witness please be -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the warnings uttered by Barac, and he sent this from the ground, especially in Bosnian Posavina and the region around Tuzla. I think that these warnings were realistic and that they were present throughout the discussion with Boban or, rather, the discussion with the faction which imposed an overall power that the HVO was supposed to take over in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask that the witness next be shown Exhibit P 03112.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we get to that, it should be pointed out for the record that on the previous exhibit, 312, Mr. Manolic did in fact speak up at the meeting. He has indicated his positions here today under oath. Perhaps he could elucidate where in the transcript is it that it verifies what he's saying here today about how he was supporting Mr. Brkic. So -- otherwise, we'll have to cover this on cross-examination. But I just point this out for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm living within time limitations as well, and I understand it's there. It is there. The Prosecution has put it into evidence. There's no hiding anything. The Court has exactly what's here, and if the Defence want to question about it further in their time, they can certainly do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's document number 134. It seems to have been a meeting that was held in the Zagorje villa on the 10th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think Mr. Karnavas and I were talking about Exhibit 31 -- P 00312.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could we have the date and the location of the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I should say perhaps for everyone in the courtroom, because perhaps that's what is causing -- again, because of time constraints, I am not going to be able to go through all the selected transcripts, so we will skip some, unfortunately, but I hope the Chamber will a chance to look at them in the future in some other context or witness, but we won't have time to go through them all with Mr. Manolic, unfortunately. The next document, Your Honour, was Exhibit 03112. It's dated the 2nd of July, 1993. It is a meeting of the Defence and National Security Council at the presidential palace. And it's -- I believe, Your Honour -- I've been told that the pagination should be consistent in all versions of this document. So page 1 of the hard copy should be the same as the page 1 on the e-court system in both Croatian and English. I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look first of all again, as we normally do, at what would be page 2 of the document. Just to confirm, this is a record of the 14th session of the Defence and National Security Council of the Republic of Croatia, held on 2 July, 1993, at the presidential palace, chaired by Dr. Franjo Tudjman. And do you see that on the list of agenda items, the first agenda item is Croatian policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that session. I think that this record is authentic, and it was -- these are the minutes recorded at that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, sir. President Tudjman begins speaking on page 2 that we were just looking at, and continues speaking for quite some pages, actually. I don't know how many pages. Never really quite -- quite -- for quite some time President Tudjman keeps speaking. Looking at page 3 of the transcript, and if I might be allowed, just in the interest of time, Mr. -- President Tudjman is indicating that he seems to be under a lot of criticism and people are asking him to do different things, and in particular at the bottom of page 3 you find this section: "First of all, criticism came from one opposition party after another, almost all opposition parties. I practically don't know of any opposition party that agreed with our state policy and there were even requests from the moderates, Budisa or Stipac personally, to dissolve, for Tudjman to take steps to abolish the community of Herceg-Bosna ..." And then beginning over to the next page, page 4, first paragraph on that page starts: "But, it was more important that in the ranks of the ruling HDZ, including council members, there was no unanimous support for the policy we implemented, if you like, which I implemented listening to all members of this council and others, but nevertheless I issued the decisions that I thought were in accord with the historic interest of the Croatian people and the Croatian state. "In that sense, it started with Boljkovac's --" excuse me for that -- "interview that explicitly attacked both our policy and people here in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then there was open disagreement in statements by Stipe Mesic, Jozo Manolic, and finally Franjo Greguric ..." Leading on to certain things, he says there was a split in the HDZ whether Tudjman was going to replace, among others, Boban, Susak, this and that. Do you see those passages, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at this, can you just in your own words tell the Judges what Mr. Tudjman -- President Tudjman was going on about in this -- in this meeting, what these comments were about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this session, President Tudjman actually defended his policies and his position against all criticism coming either from the opposition parties -- he listed all those opposition parties which advocated policies contrary to his. He also wanted to defend himself from the criticism coming from his own party, Croatian Democratic Union, whose president he was. He specifically mentioned Boljkovac as minister of interior. He mentioned me, Mesic, Greguric as well, who at one point was president of the government of Democratic Unity. In fact, he succeeded me in August of 1991. Up until the elections of 1992, he was presiding over that cabinet. Also, in one of his interviews, he expressed criticism in relation to the policies of President Tudjman. This, in a way, was consistent with my position and that of Mesic, except that he was much more moderate than I was or that then Mesic was, even though Mesic had fewer public appearances at the time than I did. He appeared on television less frequently than I did. He was especially irritated by my position, my standpoint during that period of time. Within the HDZ, one has to bear in mind that I was one of the founders of the HDZ, and I think that it is precisely this criticism which hurt him most. In this session where we constituted a minority, you can see that he invited not only members of that council but also a much broader circle of people who were not members, precisely because he wanted to recruit support for his views and thus promote the criticism aimed at me and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. If I can direct your attention, please, to page number 8. And just to confirm, this is again still President Tudjman talking. As I say, he talks for quite some time. If you see this portion, please, in the bottom half -- bottom half of the page?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "There are two main factions in the HDZ. One wants to link up with all democratic forces in Croatia, and it is oriented toward the real needs of the people. The other is working on the creation of hard-line government. I fully belong to the former." Now, my question to you, sir, is Mr. -- or President Tudjman says he belongs to the former, but based upon your experience and observations at the time, which of those two groups would you put President Tudjman in?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I believed, and I still continue to think so, that he belonged to the hard-liners, to that faction. It would have been difficult to explain him belonging to the first faction, because then at least he would have had the support of some of the opposition parties active in Croatia. And also, he would not have come into conflict with us, because I advocated a more democratic standpoint in relation to both the issues arising with Bosnia and Herzegovina and also internal issues. However, for the public, it was more acceptable for him to state publicly, "I belong to the more liberal, democratic faction."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention, please, to page 11. So toward the end of his speech -- just looking again to see if anyone has spoken up to this time. I don't think so. On page 11, President Tudjman continues: "Gentlemen, as you see, we partly discussed it before. All of this culminates in the claim that the Croatian policy we implemented, I implemented, is totally wrong and almost as some say disastrous for the Croatian people. "And now I'm going to read you a document I have received. My policy, the Croatian policy, which is not only mine, but I must say that I am the most responsible for its creation, I implemented clearly and in full or partial agreement with all of you, but we have come to a bursting point at a critical moment, to the point of whether such Croatia will survive, whether the HDZ will survive, et cetera. I implemented this policy on the basis of my own assessments and your assessments if they agreed, et cetera." You made reference earlier today that there came a point in time where you became -- you said you directed your criticisms to Susak and less directed at President Tudjman, but statements like this, did it become clear to you over time that this was indeed his personal -- not only Susak's but his personal policy?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a certain phenomenon called opportunism in politics, which is to say you that attack certain people and you keep silent about certain other people because you don't want to focus on them. So in a number of my appearances all the way up until late 1993, I attempted to create this space for manoeuvres, for the president so that he could have public appearances, give his views, and also say, "These steps were taken by such-and-such person but not by myself." However, in 1994, following the conflict he had and following the speech he gave in the parliament, he said that he took over full responsibility for the policy with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina. This completely reduced my space for manoeuvres. I could do nothing more than that. We put our cards open on the table and that was the end of any discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then, sir, for the next several pages do you recall -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are mentioning a document that I received. I think that this is the document from Hogg, foreign affairs minister of England. Is that what you have in mind? And this document was several pages long. In the session, he read out this document which was supposed to justify his policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the other hand, it was to discipline us who were against such policy, because he needed this international support to shut us up and also to weave his internal policy into the international position, and this is why this letter that came from England was so useful for him. Immediately following this, I personally started doubting the authenticity of that letter, because it seemed to me that such a confidential document as it appeared to be based on its contents, one would expect that this was -- there was some kind of foul play involved, but I couldn't really go into any further details. Could we perhaps read that letter now, or if others have it, then there is no need to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you have indeed anticipated my -- some of my questions. Mr. Tudjman goes -- President Tudjman goes on to read the letter actually in the transcript, which is -- starts at page -- for the content of the letter -- well, let's say it starts at page 12 and then goes on for several pages. And for the record, this was a letter allegedly written by Douglas Hogg to Prime Minister John Major at the time, allegedly. What did you understand President Tudjman's reason for reading this letter? You've said some -- you've mentioned something, but was he trying to use this letter to justify his policy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, the answer -- the question has been answered already, and the gentleman indicated that he wished to have the letter read. Now, this is in open court. The public is following it. I believe that the public is entitled to the reading of the letter, because from there on Mr. Manolic then comments in this very same meeting regarding the letter and the attacks or alleged attacks against him. So I think it's important for the letter to be read. And again, I believe Mr. Manolic has answered the question that was -- that's being posed now by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is a three-page letter. Read it very quickly into the transcript, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can it not count against my time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll yield my time, Your Honour. I'll yield my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It will be on Mr. Karnavas's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I would just like to add something. Your Honours, in the Croatian transcript it says that it is written by the British Prime Minister to the minister of foreign affairs, and not vice versa. I think that that's quite important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. It's a letter from John Major that is sent to the minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and I apologise if I misspoke. It is allegedly from John Major to Mr. Hogg. In reading this letter in public, Your Honour, I believe that I should state that it is the position of the British government this is a complete fabrication, but I will read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. Now the Prosecution is testifying on behalf of the Queen, you know, and the -- the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's my privilege to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I object to that. They can bring somebody from the Foreign Ministry to do so and there is language in here where even Mr. Tudjman is saying he's questioning the authenticity of it. So let's be fair. And he knows that. But he's not here on behalf of the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- it's important. Mr. Karnavas is very anxious for me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Mr. Tudjman had no doubts about the letter. You stated it wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the letter and then we'll see how things stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Dear Douglas, Thank you for your detailed report on both the current and past situation in the region of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the former Yugoslavia. As you know well from previous discussions both within the government's cabinet and on other occasions, Her Majesty's government have not changed their stand on any of the following political questions: "First, we do not agree, either now or in future, to arm or train the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina with military equipment. Second, we shall continue helping the enforcement and forceful implementation of the United Nations embargo in that region although we are well aware that Greece, Russia, and Bulgaria are supplying arms and training to Serbia, while Germany, Austria, Slovenia, and the Vatican are undertaking similar efforts on behalf of the Croatian and HVO forces within the region. "It is of paramount importance that such efforts by Islamic countries and groups are not successful on behalf of the Muslims within the region. "To this end and until the final resolution of the situation on the ground, that is until the break-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its destruction as a possible Islamic state in Europe, which will not be tolerated, we shall continue pursuing such policy. "Further, the mistake of training and arming of the Afghan fighters against the forces of the former USSR and their becoming so-called Islamic fighters now in other parts of the world and in Bosnia-Herzegovina will not --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. "... in other parts of the world and in Bosnia-Herzegovina will not be repeated with the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "This could lead to serious problems in future among the Muslim immigrant population in the European Community and North America. Please see the enclosed paper from the United States entitled 'Iran's European Springboard?', dated 1 September, 1992. Unfortunately, I do not have this paper, but it is certainly in accord with everything that has been said. "These criteria are becoming more and more relevant with common sense, and therefore special attention by our security services must be placed on the Muslim communities in the Western countries, especially here in the United Kingdom. "Third, until the situation in the former Yugoslavia is settled, we must at all cost make sure that no state deemed Muslim is allowed any say on the West policy actions in this area, particularly not Turkey. "It is therefore necessary to continue with the himba -" which someone has indicated means sham, perhaps means sham - "of the Vance-Owen peace talks in order to delay any such possible actions until Bosnia and Herzegovina no longer exist as a viable state and until its Muslim population is totally removed from its land. Continue with the himba, some of those present did not know what himba means: hypocritical, pretended, et cetera. "Although this may seem like a hard-line policy, I must insist, with you and with those that create the policy in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and in the army forces, that this is in fact a realistic policy that is in the best interest of a stable Europe in the future whose value system must remain based on a Christian civilisation and ethic. "This opinion, I must inform you, exists in any other European and North American government, and therefore we will not intervene in this region to save the Muslim population or push for the lifting of the arms embargo imposed against them. "The Muslims in the West must be made to see that they cannot oppose our views in the world, in the new world order, and that the inaction of the so-called Muslim governments in the world, which are not doing anything to oppose the destruction of the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina and which are not implementing their own promises to do something by January --" excuse me -- "15 January, 1993, given, I guess, at the Islamic Conference, the Organisation of Islamic Countries. "If the West does not save the Muslims, the Muslims in the West are totally powerless to oppose us because we control their governments, although I know that you do not think completely like ... or the minister of defence about this question, it is important in this matter that all of us have a united front against those in the parliament and in the country who have a different view, particularly after the former Prime Minister strongly attacked such a policy. I expect from all those who serve this government to submit themselves to cabinet responsibility. "Sincerely yours, John Major." Your Honour, before I leave the letter, I am going to ask this: I am going to ask the Defence at some point to advise the Chamber whether anyone suggests that this is a true and authentic letter so that we will indeed call witnesses from the British government to indicate the contrary if anyone actually suggests this is a true letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
