utterances.text: Your Honour, may I remind the Trial Chamber that the burden of proof is on the Prosecution, not on the Defence. Now, the Prosecution is introducing all of these transcripts. They're cherry picking as to what portions they like or what portions they find authentic and what portions they don't find authentic. I'm merely stating that this was in the transcript. The Trial Chamber is free to conclude whether this is an accurate and true letter, but -- but in all fairness and in keeping with the principle of completion, I think that the gentleman - that is Mr. Manolic - should be allowed to read off what his response was with respect to this particular letter, the policies expressed by the UK, if indeed they were the UK policies, and of course his response to any attacks that Izetbegovic -- that Tudjman had against him in regards to some public statements that he might have made, including I believe he had indicated that his telephone had been tapped. It's all in the same transcript. That was the whole point of it. So it's not up to me to determine whether this was an authentic or inauthentic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Manolic, the Prosecutor has just read out the letter written by the British Prime Minister to the minister of foreign affairs. Did you attend this meeting, and do you remember in any way whether the contents of this letter was disclosed to the people who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. This letter that the Prosecutor just read out was read out in its entirety directly by President Tudjman in that session. He read it out personally. I gave you the reasons. I can't further dwell on them. However, I had suspicions about the authenticity of that letter. Why would a Prime Minister from an important European country write to his foreign minister about a problem that didn't fully add up, that wasn't fully consistent with the problems that the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina had? That's why I suspected that this was not really an authentic letter written by the Prime Minister. Another thing that I wanted to say is that letters of such a nature wouldn't really reach such an audience as we were, namely the president of Croatia, which was known to have an anti-Muslim position. Why was this done? First of all, he wanted to discipline us, and he also wanted to receive, through this letter, support for his anti-Muslim policies in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, very briefly so that we don't waste too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, leaving aside the propriety of Mr. Scott representing the Queen, especially on the 4th of July, I think it would be of help to the Trial Chamber to know whether or not the letter was read during this meeting in English and was then translated, perhaps, and has now been translated back into English from Croatian, or whether a Croatian translation of the letter was read during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, President Tudjman read this letter out in English or in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Tudjman spoke English. He read this out in Croatian, because most of us did not have a command of the English language. I believe that that is why he read out a translation into Croatian. It was literally as it reads here. He had the text already translated into Croatian when he was reading it out. He wasn't doing a sight translation at the session itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If then I could direct your attention to -- well, before we do that, I'm going to go out of order, but in line with a question that Mr. Karnavas has raised, let's go straight to your -- when you make some statements. If you go to page 22 of the transcript. Hopefully we'll have time to come back. Page 22. Josip Manolic, and you start out by saying - and we really have jumped over a few things so it's not entirely in context - the criticisms that have been directed at you during this meeting already, and you say: "First, when you speak as the head of state, I'd like you to distinguish between the opposition and us who are sitting here, in both public appearances and consequences." And then he goes on. I'm going to skip down several lines, and in the following paragraph, he says: "Another thing, about my statement. I do not in the least intend to defend what I said, but my aim was to defend the policy that you inaugurated, because I started from the position that Herceg-Bosna existed and was created as a barrier to aggression and that was true. There were individual mistakes in its implementation ..." Now, did you make those statements, sir? And if there's anything you want to explain further or say more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could read the following part. Read the whole sentence. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not cross-exam. Why do I have to do it and use my time instead of having Mr. Karnavas do it during cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's my whole point, Your Honour; because it's a complete sentence. We don't stop in the middle of a thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does anyone in the courtroom not see what's on the rest of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The audience doesn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Is there anybody in the courtroom who doesn't see what is on the rest of the page? Very well. The witness cannot be asked to read the whole page on the screen, only what is important has to be pointed out. If you wish to put a question in connection with something in the text, this can be done during cross-examination. Otherwise, if we ask the witness about everything, we will stay in this courtroom for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not live to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Don't worry. You won't take that long. But there is a comma, Your Honour. The sentence goes on. I mean, we're making light of the matter, but there is a comma and the sentence goes on. Obviously, the gentleman should be given an opportunity because I believe the rest of the sentence is important. I don't mean to be obstructing the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will read the statement. Out of accommodation to Mr. Karnavas and as the agreeable Prosecutor that I always am, I would be happy to read the rest of the statement which everyone in the courtroom has already seen by now in any event, and then the witness can state his views. "There were individual mistakes in its implementation, I reduced the problem to individual mistakes, so that the general line can be defended. From beginning to end it was my idea."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us sir, now -- if Mr. Karnavas is satisfied, can you tell us anything else you want to tell us about that statement or what your position was during this meeting in response to the criticisms directed at you by President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if you look at my words in this text it is quite clear what points we agree on and what points we disagree on. This is my personal standpoint in relation to his policy and the policy being implemented towards Herceg-Bosna. I don't want to comment on myself. You don't have to read it out for my sake because I remember this text quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When it says, "From beginning to end, it was my idea," what was your idea, sir, from beginning to end?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means what I said. And thirdly, I think that there's something quite important here. I am defending the interview given by Mr. Greguric, which was also under attack because it presented a different opinion or an opinion contrary to the policy implemented by President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention over to the following page, 23. At the -- toward the bottom of that page and what you indicated as your fourth point, there's a paragraph that starts with the word "Fourth," and just in connection with the letter, the alleged letter from John Major, do you see in that letter by the -- in that paragraph, toward the end of that paragraph, you say, "I will be against such English policy"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really want to comment on that either, because I stated my position quite clearly. If the letter were true, it would not correspond to a good solution for the problems on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That is if the letter were true and, as someone said a few moments ago, if it was presented as an anti-Muslim letter, sir, you were saying that you would not have any part of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. It assumes facts not in evidence. And I think if we're going to go that route, we should read his entire answer to this question, because he starts off with -- and I don't want to go into it, but I think we need to start with, "I agree that the policy adopted by the state ..." that whole section in order to give a context rather than the Prosecutor implying what he thought at the time. I think it's quite clear over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not convinced by Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But did you say, sir -- as you in the part that I just read you to, direct your attention to in the section saying "Fourth," does it say, "I will be against such English policy"? Were those your words?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have to read the -- the entire previous part, Your Honour. You just can't read one section of it; otherwise, how do we know what's talking about? I know that we can read it, but we're asking the gentleman to now speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I'm not, Your Honour. The witness has said he knows this transcript and meeting quite well and he can say what's on the page. And Mr. Karnavas can come back and ask all the questions that he wants if he chooses to use his time that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm being forced to use my time that way. That's my only point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, it appears that in this document you are expressing a certain opinion, and your opinion is expressed as a response to what was read out to you and presented as a letter from the British Prime Minister. Based on what it says here, it would appear that you were opposing the French and British policies in this area. Tell us why you were opposed to these policies on the territory of the former Yugoslavia if, of course, you recall what you said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this is contrary to the standpoints I expressed in relation to the referendum and an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina, an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina where there were 44 per cent Muslims. When the census was taken, that was the figure. Secondly, the policy pursued by England and France might have favoured the Serbs, the Serbian policy at certain points in time, but they were not that until the end. The Washington agreements also expressed the opinions of English and French policy. So that actually goes to deny the contents of this letter that the English policy would be what is stated here. And there was a lady, a former Prime Minister, who was not advocating this standpoint mentioned in the letter. And today I'm still against such a policy, because the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot be resolved by liquidating the Muslim ethnic group in the area. Any policy, regardless of whose it was, has to take that into account or we will go back to the Middle Ages when there were events taking place in the world where entire ethnic groups and nations were wiped out. I don't think that Europe can do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we're finishing on this page, on this topic, and hopefully going back to some other entries. On this point, though, there is this continuing dialogue then between -- or some dialogue again between you and President Tudjman, and if I can direct your attention to page 24, the bottom of page 24, continuing over to the top of page 25. I suppose "Joza" is a familiar form or affectionate form of Josip, perhaps, and President Tudjman says, on the bottom of that page: "Now, Joza, you said that the policy nevertheless, that the Croatian policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina had not -- had to not only pay attention to Herceg-Bosna and Boban but also to Kljuic and Brkic, Kljuic who disappeared under Alija's fez and, excuse me, you also said that you bugged it and he repeats this today." So is this in fact the statement, sir, continued to be your position, the one you've already told us about yesterday and today, that people like Kljuic and Brkic had to be fully considered in deciding what the appropriate policy would be?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I say Kljuic and Brkic, this should be taken symbolically, because they were advocating the interests of Central Bosnia and other areas, too, not only those areas where there was an ethnically pure situation, meaning Herzegovina. Boban failed to understand this. He was pushing his own line, the line of Herceg-Bosna, to have it established in the area. He was not taking into account what would happen to all the others. That's when the conflict arose. And it was only the Washington Agreement that managed to put an end to that conflict successfully. This was not done consistently to the end, but it did stop the bloodshed, which I think is the biggest result that the Croats gained and the Muslims as well. But I do have to lay stress on the Croats, because they were in the most dire situation at the time in military terms. You may disagree with this, Mr. Praljak, but the facts show that you were in the most dire military crisis at the moment the Washington Agreement was signed. You have the right to your opinion, just as everybody else does.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On that very point, sir, if I can direct your attention now to page 17. President Tudjman speaking. "Gentlemen, I ordered - how long ago was it, when I called Defence Minister Susak and the chief of staff, General Bobetko, and told them - to take all steps for us to keep the areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina designated as Croatian according to the Vance-Owen Plan, that." And skipping to the bottom of that page: "So, gentlemen, the minister of defence and the chief of staff, please take measures. I already ordered them, to prevent this, to secure the Croatian interest in the military sense there, everything that is needed. But then again, of course, do not give it openly." And did you understand, sir, this is around -- this is July -- the 2nd of July, 1993. What did you understand to happen about the presence of elements of the Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina around this time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is evident here that President Tudjman found himself in a quandary. On the one hand, he wanted to help as much as possible by all means, and he took certain measures. I don't know what measures he took precisely, whether only military or other measures, and he ordered the chief of the General Staff, so I assume it was military measures. But then in his second sentence you see where the danger is, because he says, "Don't give assistance openly." He was afraid of pressure which might be exerted on him from the outside were he to engage militarily in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's skip the next paragraph, although there's some -- let's skip the next paragraph. "So please in the military sense and in all government departments you are to pay attention to the fact that this is about -- that in Bosnia-Herzegovina we must secure our interest in every respect." And then if I can direct your attention for -- on that point, to page 54. President Tudjman: "Anyone else? All right, gentlemen, let's finish. "With regard to sanctions, I do not think that in such a situation they pose a serious threat." He goes on to say: "I think this threat is even smaller today. But we must be careful not to give any direct cause to Serbs as an excuse for their policy. Clearly we must not do this. But at the same time we must take steps to protect Croatian interest in the territorial sense too. And, you too, please, Minister Susak, General Bobetko, see about this and meet with Herceg-Bosna leaders there, with General Praljak, Petkovic, and Ambassador Sancevic and their leaders there, with Boban and Prlic, to discuss exactly what should be done. But it goes without saying, do not lead the operation in such a way as to make a direct involvement." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This runs throughout the text: Let's go into action. Let's help Herceg-Bosna, but not so that it can be noticed and observed by external elements. This is the danger he keeps pointing out. He was a realistic politician, and he knew that the imposition of sanctions because of involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina would mean sanctions against Croatia. It would mean the isolation of Croatia. It would bring into question the very survival of Croatia as an independent and sovereign state. That's why he keeps stressing this "Don't let it be known in public. Don't let it be registered." But you will recall that the UN Security Council did register this with their famous sentence, "Elements of the Croatian army are in Bosnia-Herzegovina." This could not be denied in discussions among us, nor could it be denied in public, and least of all could it be denied in the reports being handed round in the Security Council and the UN. That was the difficulty in implementing this state policy. It wasn't so simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask the usher to please now take us to Exhibit P 08012. You have that, sir. Is this the record of a meeting, looking at the -- page 2 of the document. I hope this will be -- the page 2s will be the same in all versions, electronic and hard copy, I hope. Page 2, do you see that this is a record of a meeting on the 27th [sic] session of the Council for Defence and National Security, held on the 4th of March, 1994, chaired by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an error here. It's not 27 but 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology, Your Honour, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 37th, session, sir. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this session. It was devoted to the pre-agreement for the Washington Agreements, discussing the particular paragraphs of the Washington Agreement. We were taking our positions as regards accepting these documents. I have to point out that the definition provided by the Security Council pre-dated this, and it was a form of pressure on President Tudjman to get him to accept the Washington Agreement without any objections. And if we want to be totally objective, this was the positive side of the authoritarian nature of President Tudjman which predominated both in Croatian politics and the politics of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nobody could find the strength to oppose it. This group in Bosnia-Herzegovina was unable to resist this policy although it represented a 180-degree turn-around, because up to that point they had been waging war against the Muslims, and now they would be in a federation with those same Muslims, in peacetime. But there was no resistance. Even those who favoured the war option agreed because of the authority of President Tudjman. So they did not resist this policy but accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell the Judges a bit more, just in terms of setting the scene, if you will. By the 4th of March, 1994, the Washington Agreement was, if not entirely we would say a fait accompli, the writing was on the wall so to speak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we look still on this -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Washington Agreement was signed somewhat later. These things, however, represented preliminary material. They were discussed previously, and I think that it was at the session that they were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And still on the second page but looking at the agenda items, the agenda item 1 is "Preliminary agreement on forming Croat-Muslim federation in BH and confederation with Croatia." And then at the bottom of the page -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, it says -- let's -- "We move to the first item," and then going over to the top of page 3, it also mentions, by the way, that Mr. Prlic was also present at this meeting, which I believe you mentioned earlier; is that correct? Earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to page 4.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that during this session it wasn't just the council members. I think that there was broader attendance there and that certain officials from Herceg-Bosna were also invited. I can't remember everyone who attended, but I remember Prlic, who also took part in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we go to page 4, then. Starting about the middle -- a little above the middle of the page: "That's what I've been talking about in a message yesterday, and if somebody doesn't understand, I say why did we create Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Then I'll say it again so we could achieve the results of this politics. If we didn't have and don't have now the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, we wouldn't have the Croat-Muslim federation in Bosnia. That is, we wouldn't have the confederation of that Croat-Muslim Bosnia with Croatia. "In other words, we'll have in the sphere of Croatia, I did not say two Croatias, but we will have at least --" excuse me -- "we'll have at least half of Bosnia. And then those with big mouths or those who do not understand that I was the one who advocated division of Bosnia, can draw their own conclusion now that West is not only executing but even forcing us to accept division of Bosnia. Only, for reasons of their own, they impose on us union with Muslims ..." Can you tell the Judges, in this -- in this meeting, did President Tudjman essentially say -- try to say that the Washington Agreement was the best that could be done, that a lot had been accomplished? Because we really -- the Trial Judges will have the entire transcript, which is here, but do you recall that that is a large part of what President Tudjman was doing in this meeting, and that is selling the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in this case, when you read his entire statement, you'll see that this was his defence of the policies towards Bosnia and Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna. He doesn't want to accept this as a complete U-turn in relation to the previous preparations for the Washington Agreement, because this inaugurated peace and up until that time we had war. He was unable to accept that, because if he accepted that, later in the text you will see the statement given by Susak, "How are we going to justify the victims or, rather, the sacrifices that we suffered in that war?" This is the negative side of that policy, because at that point in time they had to acknowledge, they had to realise that this wasn't a U-turn but, rather, a continuity of the policy that they have pursued so far. To call it a U-turn would have been impossible because otherwise they couldn't justify all the sacrifices that were incurred in the conflict with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the interests of time, I'd like to direct you to page 42 of the document where you express your views on this agreement, the Washington Agreement. For the record, what happens in large part of this meeting after Mr. Tudjman -- President Tudjman talks is that there seems to be -- everyone goes around the table and expresses their view, and you -- it gets to you on page 42, and starting there: "Josip Manolic: I think that the agreement is ideal from the point of view of interest of Croatia, primarily the Croatian state, but it will liberate us and it has already liberated us. I think that the example that Gojko presented now shows that if it were not for the agreement, we would be under blockade. That's why it is ideal, primarily from the point of view of Croatian state and Croats and its interest in whole BH, and as such, I believe we should welcome it. "It's another question if the agreement could have been reached earlier, and if we could have solved this nightmare, and unannounced blockade and pressures of embargo earlier. I think that we should leave it to history and instead face the future in implementing this agreement. I think that credits for this agreement don't go to only one side, but all three sides that were involved in this. Why credits?" And Tudjman says: "Which three sides? "Manolic: Well, Americans, Muslims, that is Bosniaks, and us. Because if our interest had not matched the American interest, world interest, we would still be living miserably in war in a hopeless situation in which we found ourselves. If it had not coincided with the interest of Muslims, they certainly would not have agreed to it ..." Sir, can you tell the Judges, did you find essentially the Washington Agreement to be -- to put into effect a -- what you and Stipe Mesic, for example, had been advocating for some time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can say so with full confidence that the Washington Agreement was fully consistent with our efforts up until that time, first to avoid any conflict with the Muslims, then once it arose we wanted to put an end to it, and we wanted that to be discontinued. You see -- and there were no efforts invested either by the Croatian side or the Muslim side to put an end to this conflict earlier. International community had to get involved, the United States and other countries who took part in designing of the Washington Agreement. However, this also illustrates the persistence, just what persistence was applied, although it is completely illogical, because this clearly was a discontinuation with the policy pursued so far in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is where he and I started debating, and I think that I was right at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 3.30. We shall have a break now and resume at ten minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention, please, to page 55 of this same record, which is again, for the record, it's P 08012. And at this page -- at this point Mr. -- or President Tudjman comes back into the discussion, says: "Anyone else? (No.) Okay, let's finish this item. "Before my closing argument, a short recap on the discussion. I think it's clear from the whole discussion that everybody agrees this is useful for a Croatian nation --" again, we're talking about the Washington Agreement here -- "... useful for the Croatian nation, Croatian state, Zubak even used triumph of our politics. But also I agree that we should not use such an approach that would insist only on that. But at the same time we should affirm that this is the result of consistency of our politics. On the subject of that, hardly anyone has. Obviously Mesic and Manolic have a little different judgement. Isn't it, Stipe Mesic, that our politics paid attention on external and internal limits but our politics led active politics which led to that." And then goes on, among other things, and says, "I was the one who mainly initiated the suggestion of Cutileiro's canton solution ..." And he refers, going on to the next page, at 56, "Thus, Joza Manolic, we should talk about past, and not ... "Josip Manolic: I did not say that ... "President: No, no, but you think that we could have avoided the conflict, that it's our mistake, as you publicly said several times that it was a mistake of politics that conflict with Muslims in Herceg-Bosna happened - which is not true. And I, although I was determined, to remove Boban from the political scene exactly in order to come to that, but not because I would believe that Boban was guilty and that, as some of you said, the very idea of talking about adjoining of Herceg-Bosna would be wrong, but things have developed in such a way so that Serbia joins, and the West allows establishment of Muslim state. It is clear that adjoining Herceg-Bosna to Croatia should have been prepared." Skipping one paragraph, and then I'll just have a question for you, and it's in light of what you said a few minutes ago: "Thus it is not a turn, but consistency of our politics ..." Sir, can you further respond to this passage in terms of what you said earlier today about whether this involved consistency, as President Tudjman claimed, or I think you said a U-turn.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that anyone observing the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in Herceg-Bosna, and anyone observing the policy of Croatia, specifically that of the president, would notice the discontinuity in this policy, this U-turn. However, he could not admit, he could not accept that this was a U-turn. Rather, he termed it something that was consistent with his previous policies, because had he accepted that this was a U-turn, then -- then he would have had to confront what I was saying all along, that there should have been no conflict between the Croats and the Muslims in territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So he would have had to accept that or not accept that. I stated at the time at the meeting, and also later, that there should have been no conflict between the Croats and the Muslims. There should have been no victims, no sacrifices, and there should have been no difficulties which were inherent in that conflict. There would have been no problems. And there were a lot of problems that accompanied that situation, that accompanied Bosnia and Herzegovina and was a bit similar with the aggression used by Serbia in order to resolve the issues in Bosnia and Herzegovina that wasn't nice, that wasn't acceptable, but it was a fact. There should have been no conflict, and since there should have been no conflict, there should have been also no consequences resulting from that conflict. So even the opposition parties which were created in Bosnia-Herzegovina, created by Croats such as Komsic's civil party and some other political parties -- I think that even Kljuic established his political party. And all of these parties were opposed to the policy pursued by Mate Boban and later on by his successors, all the way up until the Washington Agreement. You see, he didn't want to admit. He didn't want to admit to Komsic either that he had advanced a proper policy. No. He's saying here that even Komsic was going along with the HDZ policy too. However, it's hard to justify it, hard in the face of all the things that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for clarification in the transcript, sir, on page 111, line 18 -- starting on line 17, it says: "He didn't want to admit to Komsic either that he had advanced a proper policy." Did you say had advanced a proper policy or an improper policy?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Komsic was looking for a solution roughly along the same terms or along the same line as Kljuic and his successor later on, and -- however, it can't be denied, it can't be said that Komsic didn't want to pursue a policy that would be in the interests of Croats in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, even though I think that later on everybody supported the Washington Agreement, which is quite significant, significant because President Tudjman also supported them and in a way promoted or, rather, supported it and in a way promoted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If we can then go, sir -- I think the final transcript that we'll have a chance to look at is Exhibit P 01325. P 01325. Sir, if you look at the second page of the document. Can you confirm that this is a meeting of the Republic of Croatia Defence and Security Council held on the 27th of January, 1993, chaired by President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the minutes from the session chaired by President Tudjman on the 27th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this transcript, sir, and we're only going to have time to refer to a few bits of it, it refers to, at the bottom of page 2 and continuing on, a letter that had come to President Tudjman from Jadranko Prlic about developments in Bosnia at this time, around the second half of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we get to that, Mr. President, could we establish whether the gentleman was present or not? It appears his name is missing from the minutes of the first page, so perhaps he can tell us whether he was at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us whether you recall being present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though some people who were not members of the council were also invited to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can just direct your attention then on to page 5, after Mr. -- the letter from Prlic is read. And Susak speaks and says: "Mr. President, I had a report this morning at 1130 hours, sent from Busovaca by Kordic and Bruno Stojic. They had cut off the Kiseljak-Busovaca road in the village of Kacuni. There have been no other developments so far." And to page 7, middle of page 7, please. Susak talking again. He says: "We have the report of General Praljak and Stojic according to which Alija does not have control over these units." And then on page 8, Susak says: "I do not know when you spoke with Boban, but I talked with him around 1100 hours this morning. "President: No, I spoke with him tonight." And one more entry before I ask you a couple of questions about this. Over on page 9, Susak again: "They are running out of materiel up there and it's difficult to deliver it. They're lacking materiel. Praljak and Stojic are organising in the south everything in their power. The general and I have done here everything that we could. We shall monitor the situation." Sir, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be good to pay attention to the date, the 27th of January, I believe. This was the period of time when these Croatian forces of the HVO found themselves in a very difficult military situation and when, in a way, they needed to be supported more strongly for them to be able to persevere in certain portions of the front. This is precisely why Susak speaks of this. Not of the difficulties but, rather, of ways and means of helping these units which were located in the areas where the HVO positions were threatened. In addition to this, there are different assessments provided by individuals and the leadership of the party, but I think that in that meeting the difficulties were discussed at length, the difficulties in which the HVO in Bosnia and Herzegovina found itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct you to one more entry on the -- page 12, toward the bottom of that page. Mate Granic was at that time the minister of foreign affairs for the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Granic was the minister of foreign affairs of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Mr. Granic says: "Mr. President, in line with your yesterday's talks with Ms. Ogata, I have spoken with Mr. Prlic and before that with Minister Susak about how to deal with international humanitarian organisations for the time being." Did you, sir -- the President of the -- of this trial asked earlier, either yesterday or today, whether information reports were coming back to Zagreb. The type of information that's being reported back here from -- letter from Prlic, reports from Stojic and Praljak, is that consistent with what you found to be the case, that Mr. Susak and President Tudjman were frequently briefed and informed on what was happening in Bosnia on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the formal, legal point of view, this was a different state. However, practically speaking, there was no border there. There existed a direct contact between the minister of defence and the president as commander-in-chief with those units or, rather, with the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, its president, and other officials. I think that when it comes to the intensity of the contact and problems, people who were direct participants would be better placed to tell you more about this. I didn't know how the letter by Prlic reached the president, whether it went through the regular channels of communication between the leadership of Herceg-Bosna and the leadership in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I thank you very much on behalf of the Prosecution for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes our time. I would like the record to reflect that I think we've used a little over five hours of our time, which means that we have come in considerably less than the estimate. I do want the record to reflect, though, that in order to do that, there's a number of exhibits that we have not been able to cover, and I know there's frequent statements about the amount of time available in the trial, Your Honour, and I just want the record to show that the Prosecution is also affected by time limits and has tried to live within those time limits, and where we can, do better than the time estimates that we have given to the Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. Can you tell us what are the numbers of the documents you wish to tender into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would -- sorry. If you would allow me, because again we have skipped, even in the course of this afternoon, various exhibits, if I could be allowed to go back through those and give those to you in the morning, I would appreciate it, the final list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask also if we could have an accounting of the pages, the number of pages of all of the documents being tendered, in light of the comment that I just heard from Mr. Scott, because I think this goes to the time limitation, because as I noted, he's picking and choosing, and we have to go through all of these documents, so that's why time limitations are not realistic in certain -- with certain witnesses. Also, we are not preventing the Prosecution from putting on his or her case. They can do so. They can take all the time they want. Now, having said that, I believe it's Mr. Praljak who would lead the cross-examination, Your Honour. And I can also state with some degree of certainty that the Defence has not been able to come to any real agreement as to the amount of time necessary, how we're going to divide the amount of time, because we all have our respective clients and our respective defences. Having said that, we're going to try to be as efficient as possible, and I believe Mr. Praljak will start off first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say without much hesitation that the Defence has managed to agree on how to use our time, yes, but I wish to know how much time will be used by whom. So please tell us, Mr. Karnavas, how much time you envisage using for the defence of your client, Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's a very difficult question to answer, and here's why: Mr. Praljak is going to go first, with Mr. Kovacic following. Depending on the areas that they're going to cover, then I would be able to give you an estimation. I mean, this is how it is, unfortunately. But I have spoken with some of my colleagues to divide parts of the topics so we don't cross over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with reference to the documents, Mr. Scott mentioned he would not present all the documents he intended to use with this witness but possibly these documents would be presented through another witness. Respecting the principle that documents are tendered through witness testimony, we feel that at this point those documents can only be marked for reference, for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to add something for Your Honour's information. Over the weekend when preparing for this witness, we had quite a lot of communication and each team has its own ideas and its own objectives in this cross-examination. However, we were unable to completely define all the topics that the four defence teams will deal with because each team feels they have quite a lot to cover. Mr. Praljak and I have a large area to cover, and for this reason it's very difficult for us to say how much time we will need. Having heard this witness, Your Honour, you yourself can see that this is a very important part of the indictment, the theory of joint criminal enterprise. A lot of details have been referred to. A lot of material has been dealt with. I can only say that our questions will be relevant and they will not be repetitive, because even though we have not managed to fully define our respective areas of examination, if one Defence counsel puts a question that others had intended to put, they will certainly strike that question off their list of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I wish to say something for clarification. We now have an hour. We will begin, but in the morning, before the beginning of the day's session, we will give you complete information as to how much time each team will need. We didn't know how much time Mr. Scott would use until the end of the day and what documents he would tender into evidence, which is why we could not reach a precise agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott. I was just about to ask you something. We have here all these documents, and with the exception of the book written by the witness, they are all minutes from sessions attended by the witness. He recognised these minutes, he stated that he attended those meetings and sessions, and on the basis of this, you can ask that they be received into evidence unless among these minutes there are some you intend to introduce through another person who attended these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for that. Yes, in fact I think the witness would confirm -- I suppose I should have done that, but again I was trying to use time very, very efficiently -- that the witness can confirm that as to the documents -- transcripts that were marked for this witness, the ones, whether we've gotten to them or not, these are all meetings that he attended and participated in, and I believe he would be able to say -- I'm confident he would say that. I suppose if the -- if we were to go through those and do that, each one with him, we can do that. I can offer -- I can make an offer of proof to the Court that would be his evidence. That's point -- that's one point, Your Honour. I was also going to make another point but I think you raised a more important point first. If the Chamber wants me to go back through all the -- the additional remaining transcripts and have him confirm his involvement in these various meetings, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do that, but I think it would be best if you were to go in order. For example, take document 37, the session of the 8th of June, 1991. Were you there? Yes. Second, session 68 of the 12th of November, 1991. The witness will say, "I was there," or, "I wasn't there." You can deal with it very quickly. So I will ask you to do so now, and after that we will give the floor to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. If I can just get some assistance from the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you confirm -- you heard the discussions, I think, between the counsel and the Chamber in the last few minutes. You've looked specifically at -- and I'm sorry I didn't keep a separate list of these with me. You looked at a transcript of a meeting dated the 8th of June, 1991, which you specifically gave evidence on. You also gave specific evidence on a meeting on the 12th of November, 1991. I believe you also gave evidence on Exhibit P 00134, a transcript of the 10th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. To be honest, I wasn't prepared to do this in a systematic way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of some assistance, Your Honour. I assume the Prosecution intends to introduce all of the documents they indicated they would go through with this particular witness. It might save some time if, perhaps overnight, they could come up with a list. You know, that would save some time. We can get into the cross-examination. I'm perfectly willing to accept the offer of proof made by the Prosecution, but I do agree with the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the list is presented tomorrow, all right. That will be submitted tomorrow. It's sufficient for you to take the list you have already handed us and simply update it, and say which were the sessions which he attended, plus the book. The Defence will also be ready, and we will then save time. If you recall, we have stated previously that as a rule, exhibits are tendered through witnesses. If these are minutes from a session that the witness attended, there is no reason not to receive it into evidence. I will now give the floor to Mr. Praljak, but let me first say something to Mr. Manolic. Mr. Manolic, we are now entering the stage of cross-examination. Generally speaking, cross-examination is very difficult. The questions put to you might be irritating to you, but please try to remain calm and answer the questions calmly, even if they irritate you. If you have the impression that the question was put to you in an aggressive manner, don't get excited. Remain calm. This is not an arena, and it is not gladiators who are participating in these proceedings. Everybody has to remain calm. Every question that is put is put for a reason. It's up to you to answer each question. Mr. Praljak, you have understood me. I believe I can count on you to respect all this. Just please tell us how much time you envisage you need. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Mr. President, there are two kinds of examination and two kinds of witnesses. One kind is a simple mathematical process. The witness says one thing, you answer, he replies. The testimony of Mr. Manolic, who was for a long time on intimate terms with President Tudjman and the second-ranking man in Croatia, has opened up a whole range of issues. Translated into physics, this is like saying solve the quantum problem of the law of gravitation. This, unfortunately, is not simple. Endeavouring for months to understand what would be the relevant questions in these proceedings, I attempted to save time, because I had a constant feeling of guilt, fearing that I was abusing the patience of the Court and the witness but also concerned for my right to my defence and my dignity, which I have not abandoned. As Mr. Manolic has put forward a number of theses about politics, about the link between politics and crimes, about the functioning of power and government, about stories and rumours that went round and so on, I cannot at this point in time tell you how long it will take me to put the questions to which I must receive the answer. If one question alone is not sufficient, I need to get an answer. Anyway, as Mr. Manolic and I have known each other for a long time, we were in politics together from 1989, I can put a very relevant question. Does Mr. Manolic know, has he heard, was he informed, and let me tell you that over a long period during the war Mr. Manolic was at the head of all the intelligence services in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is this correct, Mr. Manolic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me from when to when.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you stopped being the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia until you became the Speaker of the House of Counties, you were the chief of all the intelligence services. You were in the office for the protection of the constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Continue, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is the following: Did Mr. Manolic, as the best informed person, along with President Tudjman, ever anywhere hear that Slobodan Praljak, as a volunteer and a commander in Sunja in political life, as the commander of the HVO, as the assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia, ever by word or deed, by intention or any public act or speech, do anything anywhere at any time that would be contrary to any law or any ethical and moral norm? Because then Mr. Manolic could tell Their Honours it happened here at such-and-such a place, at such-and-such a time, in such-and-such a manner. If his answer, however, was no, then I could sit down. But we would not then be resolving everything that has been said here about politics, about the functioning of government, about the conditions in which all this took place. We are talking here with Mr. Manolic as if we were in a test tube, as if there were no people being killed, wounded, no refugees, no fear, no pain, no desperation, no hatred. Everything is peaceful, quiet. We are in the corridors, and yet I'm putting the following question: In this huge game of great minds, meetings, conclusions, the question remains of my mother living in Mostar, asking, "Who is going to protect me? Will the same fate befall me that befell those people in Vukovar? Will I be killed? Will my throat be slit? Will I be expelled from my home?" There were tens of thousands of people putting the same questions. In the introductory part here --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point. This has gone on long enough. This is not the time for opening speeches or closing arguments. I think cross-examination should begin. The Chamber has asked Mr. Praljak to put a question and I think he should put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, go ahead. Please start your questioning of the witness. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I will, and it will go on until we finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: With respect to the transcripts, Mr. Manolic, when meetings were held in President Tudjman's office, meetings of the Defence and National Security Council, was the purpose of these meetings to put forward all theses, to have a free discussion? Was this treated as a conversation similar to conversations that take place in one's home, among one's friends, in a cafe, in the street? Is the conversation free and people put forward even theses they don't abide by simply to see what can be put on the table? Was it like this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. When you look at the minutes, you will see that the meetings lasted from one to two hours at the most. You are limited in time, and you were also limited by the agenda. One did not stray beyond the agenda. So your idea about a drawing room discussion where one can discuss all kinds of matters, from virginity to crime, that doesn't hold water. My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question was not about straying beyond the agenda. What I said was that the items on the agenda could be discussed much more freely just as in the cabinets and behind closed doors in all governments and all states, discussions are much freer than the public statements made later by any of the participants of the meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct either, because at that point in time when minutes were taken, or the transcript as we call it now, the intention of the transcript was not to be made public. It was intended for that circle to note down the standpoints and ideas presented. We don't need to discuss this at length. You can see it in the very text of the transcript. Beyond that, I couldn't go. You can say whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you told me quite correctly that these transcripts were not intended to be made public.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The transcripts were not later given to the participants in the meeting for them to read through, correct, or authorise? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I and not only I but none of the participants ever saw the transcripts that we have available now. None of us ever authorised those transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean to say that there was a stenographer taking minutes, just like the court reporter here, who types out everything that was said in the room where the session was held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't go into the technology, but I assume that a lot of this was recorded on an audio recording and then transcribed from the tape and copied, transformed into a text. But I can say neither yes nor no because I can't go into the technical aspect. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did every participant in every meeting know that he was being recorded or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you think or do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, because I didn't ask any of the participants whether they knew they were being recorded or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president sometimes said, "Be serious. This is going to be recorded." But people knew more or less, and I don't think you can see that in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was it the custom among journalists or other people to draw a sharp distinction between speech, which includes gestures, mind, body language, tone of voice, laughter and so on, and what is transcribed of all this? Is there a significant difference between the spoken and written word, or can there be a significant difference?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, yes, but at these sessions this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have you dealt with communications, language and speech, in order to be able to say so clearly that there is a theoretical difference but it didn't happen there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't happen there. I'm testifying to what happened. I'm not testifying about the philosophical discussion of what could or could not have happened in theory. We have to be practical now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, may I ask both of you gentlemen, please, you are speaking in your mother tongue, and you have to think about the interpreters. And first of all, both of you should slow down and bit, and secondly, please wait until the interpreters will finish with your statements and then of course to start and reply, to put the question and reply. But please be aware of the fact that for you it is very easy to talk in your mother tongue, but it is not easy for the interpreters to translate it. I would like very much to thank you for following this advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for cautioning us. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Why call each theoretical dispute - I'm now quoting your words - philosophising? Because philosophising means search for truth. I'm asking you, Mr. Manolic, is it true that everywhere in the world, when one wants to use a document which was secretly recorded, that this document is then given to somebody to confirm it, to authorise it? I'm saying this, that there is a significant difference between oral communication and written communication. Oral communication containing also gestures and all other body language. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you that there may be a difference there. I fully agree with you there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line with what Mr. Praljak has talked about, Mr. Praljak mentioned a secret recording. When you met, was the person taking the minutes physically present or were you recorded with audiotapes and you did not know that this recording was taking place, or was there a stenographer in the room and present together with Mr. Tudjman and all the other people whose names were on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't tell you that with full certainty, but I can tell you with full certainty that I saw no person taking minutes there in the room or sitting at the table, which means that there was a recording equipment and that the personnel doing that was in another room. I can tell you that with full certainty. But it seems to me that Mr. Praljak would like to draw this conclusion. Namely, he wants to question the authenticity of these transcripts and to which extent they properly may be used in such trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what my question is about. Since yesterday, we've been spending a lot of time looking at these documents and what has been said in the presence of Mr. -- of President Tudjman. When you were asked -- my question is: Did you know that what you were saying was being recorded? You were at the head of the intelligence service, so you must have known something about this. So when you addressed President Tudjman or spoke before him, did you know that what you were saying was being recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I never wondered about that, nor did I ever ask the president whether that was being recorded or not. That was his own matter and that of his inner circle, the technical personnel that he had arranged this with. I wasn't interested in it. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, it doesn't matter whether you were interested in this or not. I'm putting forward a claim here that you can deny if you wish without wondering about the objective of my claim. Except when President Tudjman explicitly stated that the meeting was recorded, in all other cases those attending meetings, including myself, didn't know that the meeting was recorded. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody knew about this. That's the essence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, this is what we're trying to establish here. People didn't know unless it was explicitly stated that any meeting was recorded. Thank you very much. Mr. Manolic, I'm now putting questions, and we need to move at a certain pace. The principle of volition means that occasionally our emotions, which may arise, that we may sometimes keep them to ourselves and control them. For example, in the middle of the attack on Croatia, Croatia is on fire, and then a decision is taken within the Security Council to impose embargo and to deny a right to an entire nation. Then under those circumstances I will fully acknowledge before this Trial Chamber that very passionate emotions may rise within me, emotions in relation to big powers such as France, the United States, China, Russia, and so on, because I think that it's unfair, I think that it's improper. I think that it's uncivilised. I think that it's contrary to all proper norms to deny a nation a right to self-defence and to allow somebody to go ahead killing them. Please let me put my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is no question here. Once again we're back to making speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please avoid lengthy speeches. This is in your own interest. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] In my view, it is essential to establish whether I, under those circumstances -- when I'm in a room with my wife, when I know that I am not recorded, whether I under such circumstances may utter words, and these were not publicly uttered, may utter words which then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] -- may be used in court against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Praljak's views whether it's essential or not. He's not making those judgements. If he'd like to put a question to the witness, he can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, if I may be of some assistance. I think this is very relevant, you know, to what Mr. Praljak is trying to achieve, and that is if no one knew that they were being tape recorded, then obviously they would not be guarded in what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] All right. We have concluded with this. We may move on. Actually, I can round up my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, when a lot of blood was shed, Croatia was on fire, can a man control his emotions under such circumstances? Is a man entitled to such emotions, and do they represent a crime? Did you experience such emotions yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, as regards those sanctions that were imposed against Croatia at the time, I can agree with you, but that's not what we're discussing here now. We're not discussing whether it was justified for sanctions to be imposed against Croatia at that time. I don't think that this is the matter that is relevant here. And I think that you used up some half an hour, and we could have concluded this very quickly, just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I'm not your student.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not your student either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm not your party student. Please allow me to defend myself to the best of my abilities. I'm not attending a party school in Kumrovec now, a party school of the League of Communists, therefore I ask that you answer my questions. This is your role at this moment. In the book that I'm holding here, there are 227 documents, documents of President Tudjman, Croatian government, Croatian parliament, signed by them during these events, mostly pertaining to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Karnavas and his Defence team have all of these documents in English. I will very quickly get to the questions. On the 27th of February, 1991 - 27th of February - a declaration was adopted on the state sovereignty and indivisibility of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe such a document exists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: This declaration was adopted because the representatives of the Muslim nation in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and representatives of the Croatian nation in that Assembly voted for this declaration. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I as a witness before this Tribunal cannot go into what was going on in certain parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I can only testify about the events in which I personally participated. I can only describe to you what was happening there at the time where I was. Now you're trying to draw me into Bosnia-Herzegovina. I only visited that region once or twice, when I went to Sarajevo. Nor did I participate in various discussions about these problems. Therefore, please spare me, because the only answer I can give you is no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'm confused now.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So am I.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You came here to testify, and you have been testifying the whole time about the relationship between the Croatian policy, or, rather, the involvement of Croatia in the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So how, then, can you claim that you know nothing about that, you have no idea, you didn't visit the region at the time, and generally you're not interested?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reason for me to know about the documents adopted by Bosnia-Herzegovina in any of its bodies. That's not what I'm testifying about. I'm testifying about the material contained in this book and I'm also testifying about the transcripts and their contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic. Mr. Manolic, please look at the Bench when you answer the question. So please listen to the question and look at us when you answer. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I cannot but tell you that this declaration for which the Croats voted, there were 44 representatives of the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you accuse the HDZ of working in order to break this country apart. So I'm asking you now whether this document says the following: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a sovereign unitary indivisible democratic state of all citizens residing therein. Item 2: "The borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina are not subject to change." And only towards the end do they mention the rights of the people, which is a bit strange. And you never heard of this document; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nor do I wish to go into this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 29th of June, 1991, President Alija Izetbegovic, when discussing the future of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, came up with the six items. Are you aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time Mr. Izetbegovic asked the US Secretary of State, Mr. James Baker, and now I'm quoting: For the international community to focus on Bosnia-Herzegovina, because a civil war, which is a realistic threat, would be sure to break out first in this republic. Baker agreed with that. This is what Izetbegovic added. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this question was never discussed at the meetings of Defence and National Security Council where I was present, so once again my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 7th of July, 1991, the Brioni Declaration was adopted, which reads as follows: "The participants of the third round of negotiations between the delegation of the European Community and the Yugoslav representatives adopted a document on peaceful resolution of the crisis." And then further on it says: "The peoples of Yugoslavia are the only ones who can decide on their own future. The negotiations must start urgently, no later than the 1st of August, 1991. All aspects of the future of Yugoslavia without any preconditions and based on the principles contained in the final document from Helsinki and in the Paris Charter and so on need to be implied." Brioni is located in Croatia. Are you aware of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that this meeting was held. I personally didn't participate in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But at that point in time you were the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you give me the time frame, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The 7th of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th of July. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you as Prime Minister, in a situation where the fate of the people whom you are leading is being discussed.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered your question. I told you that I was aware of the meeting and of what transpired there. That's what I replied. What else do you want?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In The Hague, the place where we are now, on the 6th of August, 1991, the European Community adopted a Declaration on Yugoslavia. This was the declaration of the ministers of 12 States. At the time, the EC had only 12 members. So they, the 12, urgently demand the Presidency of Yugoslavia to organise a conference on the future of Yugoslavia. They were prepared to organise such a conference themselves. Such negotiations ought to be based on the principle that any changes of internal or external borders are not acceptable and that the rights of minorities need to be guaranteed in all republics. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document was not presented at the sessions which I attended.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's quite sufficient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said a while ago that at the time you were Prime Minister a meeting is convened in The Hague and a declaration is made by the ministers of the EC, which at the time comprised 12 Member States. The declaration is about Yugoslavia on a future conference on Yugoslavia to be held in the future, and you're telling us that you did not know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is one to be informed and quite different to participate. I did not take part in that. I think that this resolution was treated in Yugoslavia or, rather, was treated by the Presidency of Yugoslavia. They discussed it. If you give me the date, then I will be able to give you this more accurately. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's the 6th of August, 1991. Mr. Manolic, I'm asking you now, were you aware of this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was aware of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think that our minister participated in some way in all this, but afterwards it was not raised in the sessions in which I participated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: My second question: Did Mr. Franjo Tudjman, the president of the Croatian state, take an active part in the creation of each one of these documents?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he participated quite intensively in all these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that doesn't mean --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Manolic. Please be correct towards me.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Answer my question without adding anything. You have explained everything you had to explain when Mr. Scott was putting questions to you. I am asking you questions in the way you wanted them asked, whether you knew something, whether you didn't. As to what somebody else was doing or thinking or what you thought they were doing or thinking is not relevant here. The Court is here to establish facts, and we shall keep opinions for some other time and place. Thank you. Are you aware that on the 2nd of August, 1991, the Serb-Muslim historical agreement was signed in Belgrade between Muhamed Filipovic and Radovan Karadzic? In this agreement, the Serbs and the Muslims discussed without the Croats and tried to agree on their co-existence. Do you know of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've only heard that there was such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 5 of this agreement, it says: "We express our interest for the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina to live with us in full equality, and we invite them to accede to this agreement regardless of the position of the Republic of Croatia within or without Yugoslavia. The Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina are a fully equal nation." Mr. Manolic, if you were a Croat from Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you consider such an agreement to be a kind of treason towards the Croats who are being offered some solutions in Article 5 after all the discussions had taken place?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed that agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 8th of October, 1991, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia adopted a decision on severing state and legal links with the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You know about this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I will read to you points 4, 5, and 6. "4. The Republic of Croatia recognises the independence and sovereignty of the other republics of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia based on the principle of reciprocity and is ready, with those republics with which it is not engaged in an armed conflict, to establish and develop friendly, political, economic, cultural, and other relations. "5. The Republic of Croatia as a sovereign and independent state guaranteeing and ensuring fundamental human rights and the rights of national minorities guaranteed explicitly by the general declaration of the United Nations the final document of the Helsinki Conference, the documents of the OSCE and the Paris Charter as part of the European integration processes is ready to enter into interstate and regional democratic associations with other countries. "6. The Republic of Croatia will continue the process of establishing mutual rights and obligations in relation to the other republics of the former SFRY and the former federation." That's what it says here. Could something like this have been adopted without the express support of Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you are reading a declaration to me which has nothing to do with these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
