utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You told the Court and all of us today a number of incredible things about me, logical absurdities, showing ignorance, and I have the right to read 227 documents which were created under the leadership and influence and political power of Franjo Tudjman, who you say was at the head of a criminal organisation.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please. I will go through them and thereby demonstrate that the continuity of such a policy can be seen in every document everywhere within the framework of the actual circumstances prevailing at the time. With people who are suffering and being killed, with a state organisation that was falling apart, taking the only possible course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I would like to interrupt you here, and I apologise for it. You just stated here on lines 21 and 22 that -- it was your question directed to the witness: "You told the Court and all of us today a number of incredible things about me, logical absurdities showing ignorance," et cetera. So frankly, in my view it would be a better way of asking questions if you would refer back to those "number of incredible things about me." If you really felt that way, please ask concrete questions from the witness, from Mr. Manolic. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. This is because Mr. Manolic is interrupting me, trying to explain to me what I'm supposed to do. I will not do this again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On the 8th of November [as interpreted], 1991, the parliament of the Republic of Croatia adopted conclusions about the aggression on the Republic of Croatia. "4. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Montenegro are invited not to allow the use of their state territory for the waging of a war against the Republic of Croatia. "5. All States, especially Member States of the European Community and the United Nations are invited to establish diplomatic relations with the Republic of Croatia. The Republic of Croatia will continue participating in the work of the conference on Yugoslavia in The Hague organised by the Member State of the European Community." Tomorrow I will show you a map showing all the places in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from which the territory of the Republic of Croatia was attacked. Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Manolic, answer.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not follow the military operations in detail, so please don't draw me into individual events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, you say that that has nothing to do with it. Mr. Praljak is putting questions to you because it is important to him. We, the Judges, don't see what his idea is yet, but he certainly has a line of questioning. If it has nothing to do with it, Mr. Praljak will have wasted a lot of time. However, we wish to think that it does have a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I correct the transcript. The document in line 21, page 139, it says the 8th of November. It was actually the 8th of October, and Mr. Praljak did say the 8th of October. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, this was adopted by the Croatian parliament of which you were a member. It was not fabricated by Praljak. The parliament said, "We are being attacked from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and from the territory of Montenegro." Mr. Manolic, the Prime Minister cannot tell me before the Court that his country, in Dubrovnik, in Zadar, in Sibenik, in Slavonski Brod and in the area of Vukovar was being attacked from Bosnia-Herzegovina. You don't know this.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know this, but why do you need to start showing me all these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused is asking you whether Croatia was being attacked from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Please answer that it was or that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it was attacked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he forgot to mention Serbia. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I haven't forgotten Serbia, but we are dealing with Bosnia-Herzegovina now. Did you, as the Prime Minister of a country that was under attack, with a third of its territory under occupation, hundreds of thousands of people expelled from their homes, did you send a letter to Mr. Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency of the state from whose territory the attacks were being launched, to ask him what he had undertaken, what he was about to undertake or intended to undertake to prevent this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've got your dates confused now. If you say that was the 8th of October, at that time I was not the Prime Minister, so it was not within my purview to communicate with the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I assume that President Tudjman certainly communicated that to him, but it's only an assumption on my part. I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the attack occurred, didn't the security council convene to see whether an official letter would be sent from the Republic of Croatia to President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this can be found in the transcripts nor do I remember our discussing this. This was something for the minister of defence and the General Staff to deal with, and also the president as the Supreme Commander. I wish Mr. Praljak would ask me those things that he has characterised as absurd or impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, please go on. We have five minutes left. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic is saying that the attack from one country on another is a matter for the General Staff and the generals and not a matter for the parliament or the cabinet. If the generals were to act on their own initiative to prevent the murders of several hundred civilians in Slavonski Brod and 27 children - and I showed Their Honours this - if they had sent the army out on their own initiative to prevent this massacre, then we would be speaking about the Croatian army in another state, the rights and legitimacy of the government in Sarajevo. And all this is all right, but the parents of those children would also require answers from those talking about legitimacy. Is what I'm saying correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're acting as if you were at a political rally where one has to speak of threats to the state and so on. You're not mentioning the institution which was supposed to respond.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Manolic. You were the second ranking man in the state, on intimate terms with the top man in the state. You were a friend who visited him in his home. So in God's name, how did you react to all this? Did you call up the cabinet as a Member of Parliament? Did you ask that something be done? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was neither in the government nor was I in the parliament. I was in a bureaucratic position, collecting information and supplying the president with that information. He and the other institutions that were supposed to respond did respond. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am finished for today, but I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, you said you would continue. Please tell us, how much time will you need tomorrow? You said, "I will continue." How much time do you need for this? Because you're referring to 227 documents. I hope you're not going to read 227 documents, because we'd have to be here for the next 25 years if you did this. How much time do you intend to use tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I don't know how these 227 documents, which go to deny the claims by the Prosecutor and all the witnesses -- I don't intend to read them out, but I want to have them at the disposal of the Court in English and French, because I'm fully convinced that, based on these documents, Your Honours will reach the decision I expect. So how can these documents be introduced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic, there will be 227 documents tendered into evidence for the Defence of Mr. Praljak. Please draw up a list. I think that you have agreed with Mr. Praljak to draw up such a list, unless you are having a problem. Please tell us, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. There is no problem. The plan is for all the documents. There may be some which are not strictly necessary, but they almost all are. They are in this book which is a good practical thing, exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then the best thing would be to tender the book into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the idea. Of course, the question of translation remains, but we will deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 20 past 5.00. We shall continue at 9.00 tomorrow, sir. As I said yesterday, in the meantime you must not have contact with anyone. I wish you all a good evening, and I will see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of July, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.18 p.m.,
